body:
Hi,

You likely have seen that in dev mode things work fine. That's because the page is rendered on demand.

When you build, the page may be pre-rendered. During pre-rendering, there's no incoming request, so we cannot resolve any query parameters. To get around this, you have to use a Suspense wrapper, so that the part of the UI that uses the `useSearchParams` hook, is deferred to the client. Note that pre-rendering outputs a ready HTML page.

When you start, if the page is a so called, `dynamic`, `on-demand` SSR page, then `useSearchParams` has access to the search params, as one would expect. Otherwise, if the page was pre-rendered, then no SSR happens, only serving of static assets.

- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-search-params

> Good to know: In development, all pages are rendered on-demand, so useSearchParams doesn't suspend. However, pre-rendering a [static page](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering#static-rendering) that worked in development will fail the build if useSearchParams is used in a Client Component that isn’t directly or indirectly wrapped in a Suspense boundary.

Lastly `use client` doesn't mean `client render` only. Client Components are what we've had up to this point, even in Pages Router. In fact in Pages Router query params have also some special behavior when pre-rendering happens. 

In other words, even with `use client` a component might be ssr'd, in the default rendering pass anyway.

- https://github.com/reactwg/server-components/discussions/4
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#on-the-server

> Client Components and the RSC Payload are used to [prerender](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/partial-prerendering#how-does-partial-prerendering-work) HTML.

So what you can do here, is either: 
- opt-out from pre-rendering
- pre-render but wrap the Client Component that has `useSearchParams` with `Suspense`, 
- or collect the `searchParams` from a parent server component page. 

For the first, you can make your `page.tsx` like:

```tsx
import { connection } from 'next/server'
import { CallbackPageUI } from './callback-ui'

export default async function Page() {
   await connection() // opt-out from pre-rendering
   return <CallbackPageUI />
}
```

And move your `CallbackPage` component into the a `callback-ui.tsx` file next to the `page.tsx`, for example. 

I wonder if in your case you may want the `server component` result, depends on your intention. 

I've been dropping improvements to the error page and documentation for this hook though.
author: icyJoseph

body:
`"use client"` means the component's code will also run on the client (and probably uses hooks and has some kind of interactivity).

That doesn't mean it doesn't get rendered on the server. All your components are server-rendered in Next.js (SSR pass).

Server rendering has two modes:
1. Prerendering (static or partial) that happens during build.
2. SSR that happens on request time.

The parts of the page that are completely static (or depend on statically derived information, like route params), are rendered once and cached.

The parts of the page that are dynamic (depend on search params or headers, or cookies, etc), need to be wrapped in order for Next.js to know that they need to be rendered on demand.

That's the rule. If you follow it you'll be fine and you get amazing performance thrown in for free.

A workaround is to not `useSearchParams`, at all, and try to read searchParams from `new URL(document.location.href)` in a `useEffect` like SPA's do.

body:
Yeah this setup makes sense, great work and congrats on the site's traction. Using the build ID to namespace your assets is a good way to make sure old HTML points to the right JS chunks. The main trade off is how many old builds you want to keep around before cleaning them up since storage will creep up fast.

For the KV side I would lean on lazy revalidation like you described instead of trying to invalidate everything on each deploy. That scales better when you are talking millions of pages. The only real gotcha I have seen is forgetting to update cache keys when you change how you generate pages which can leave stale data hanging around.

Overall it looks maintainable as long as you have a cleanup policy and some automation around invalidation.
author: hyattc1

body:
Thanks for your feedback. 

I wonder why Nextjs / Vercel does not offer this out of the box. ISR which comes closest to this is rather useless if you have to purge all cache on every build.

Do you happen to know an elegant way to solve the issue with RSC requests when users navigate between pages? It seems rather impossible to cache these between page changes.
author: fxmb

body:
ISR gets you part of the way there but it falls short when you have to invalidate everything on each build. With what you've said so far, I believe Vercel optimizes for the simpler case, smaller sites with fewer pages where global invalidation is not as painful, and leaves the more custom caching setups to teams that need it.

For RSC requests, there really is not a perfect built in solution yet. Since they are tightly coupled to the app router and the current build, caching them between navigations is tricky. The closest thing to an “elegant” approach I have seen is to treat them like API responses, put them behind KV or edge caching with a short TTL so you cut down on repeat fetches without risking users seeing stale data for long. Some people also cache them per build ID the same way you are handling static chunks, but then you still need a cleanup policy. 

This isn't easy stuff, wishing you luck as you continue to develop this. Right now it is more about layering your own caching strategy on top. Not as nice as having it built into Next, but it is what seems to work in practice.

If that clears things up, feel free to mark it accepted so others can find it too.

body:
The problem usually comes up because Next.js tries to serve static files relative to the domain it’s running on. When you put it behind a load balancer, those requests can get pointed at the LB domain instead of the Cloud Run service.

A couple things you can try:
- In next.config.js, set an assetPrefix that matches your Cloud Run service URL
- Double-check that the load balancer is rewriting paths the way you expect
- If you’re using a custom basePath, make sure that lines up too.

Easiest way to confirm is open the Network tab and see which files are 404’ing. That will usually show you if it’s just a prefix mismatch.

Turbopack in `next dev` must configure inotify watchers for every relevant file or directory in your source code and in `node_modules`, which can create a large number of watchers. Most Linux distributions set these limits to very large values by default, but this may not be true on your system.

body:
Hey everyone 👋

This error —

Module [x] was instantiated because it was required from module [y], but the module factory is not available. It might have been deleted in an HMR update.


— usually means that Turbopack’s Hot Module Reload (HMR) is trying to use an outdated client chunk while the dev server has already rebuilt a new version. Essentially, the browser’s cache and Turbopack’s module graph get out of sync.

Here’s what’s going on and how to fix it 👇

🧠 Why It Happens

When a file is moved, renamed, or deleted, Turbopack sometimes doesn’t fully invalidate its dependency graph.

The browser may still hold on to stale .next/static/chunks/*.js files if cache headers aren’t correctly set to no-store, must-revalidate.

On the next hot reload, Turbopack can’t find the old module factory — leading to the “factory not available” error.

✅ Steps to Resolve

1️⃣ Force No-Cache Headers for Chunks
Make sure your .next/static/ assets have the following headers during dev:

Cache-Control: no-store, must-revalidate


If you’re behind a proxy or CDN (like in a monorepo setup), ensure these headers aren’t being overwritten.

You can confirm in Network → Response Headers in DevTools — if you see max-age, you’re likely caching old chunks.

2️⃣ Clear .next Between Runs
Turbopack sometimes holds stale graph metadata between runs. Run:

rm -rf .next
pnpm dev


before restarting.

3️⃣ Avoid Moving/Deleting Files During Active HMR
File deletions or renames (especially across nested folders) are a known trigger. Restart the dev server after structural changes.

4️⃣ Disable React Compiler (If Enabled)
Some devs reported conflicts when React Compiler or custom instrumentation is turned on:

experimental: {
  reactCompiler: false
}


Try disabling it temporarily to confirm.

5️⃣ Monitor Turbopack’s Logs
Run with:

NEXT_DEBUG=true pnpm dev


You’ll get detailed logs about which modules are being invalidated and rebuilt — useful to confirm whether it’s a caching mismatch or internal graph issue.

🧩 In Summary

This is not usually caused by your fetch() or API caching — it’s about static chunk caching in dev mode.

Ensure .next/static files aren’t cached, clear .next, and restart after moving files.

If you can consistently reproduce it, the Next.js team can use that repro to improve HMR stability in future Turbopack releases.

✅ TL;DR Fix:

rm -rf .next
clear browser cache
ensure "Cache-Control: no-store, must-revalidate"
restart dev server


After this, HMR errors like
“factory is not available, it might have been deleted in an HMR update”
should stop appearing.

Hope this helps stabilize your dev setup! 🚀

body: I dug into my repo and I think the culprit is our service worker in dev. We register `/sw.js` unconditionally and it uses a cache‑first strategy for script/style requests, which includes `.next/static/chunks`. That can easily serve stale chunks after HMR updates, causing the `module factory is not available` error. There’s no headers() override for _next/static in dev either, so SW cache wins. Likely fix is to skip caching _next or disable SW caching entirely in dev.

body:
The problem is one of execution flow in Next.js:

If your route handler uses a try...catch block to return an error, Next.js sees this as a handled execution.

The onRequestError callback only fires on a truly uncaught exception that bubbles up to the network layer.



trigger onRequestError while controlling the response:

Stop using return NextResponse.json({ error: '...' }, { status: 400 }) inside your catch block. This prevents onRequestError from ever running.

Instead, create and throw a custom error inside your route handler's catch block. This ensures an uncaught exception fires the onRequestError function.

In your onRequestError function, check the type of the thrown error and return the custom NextResponse there.

body:
This looks like an internal issue with Turbopack (Next.js's underlying engine) when compiling the App Router's structure, often related to CSS or file resolution.

**Possible fixes** 

- Delete Cache and Reinstall: This is the most common fix for cryptic Turbopack errors.
- Restart the dev server (npm run dev --turbo).
- Check globals.css (or CSS Imports): Many similar "Failed to write app endpoint" errors trace back to an issue compiling the main CSS file.
- Remove --turbo: Since this is a known unstable feature, running without Turbopack may be necessary.
- Check File Paths (Monorepo): If you are using a monorepo (e.g., Turborepo, pnpm workspaces), the issue could be Turbopack's difficulty resolving symlinked paths.
- Upgrade to Canary: If the error persists, update Next.js to the absolute latest canary version to see if a recent Turbopack fix resolves it.

body:
I've had this problem before

This is a very common issue on Windows machines, especially when using Package Managers like pnpm or Yarn (PnP mode) alongside Cloud Sync services (like OneDrive). The error points directly to a file system lock or permission issue during a read operation.

The core problem is that Turbopack is timing out trying to read a file (less.js) that is potentially being synced or locked by OneDrive. 

**this is my usual checklist:**

- Exclude node_modules from OneDrive Sync: The quickest fix is to ensure the entire node_modules folder is excluded from OneDrive's synchronization. OneDrive locking files in this heavy-I/O directory is the primary cause of the os error 426 timeout.

- Clean Cache and Reinstall

- Move the Project: if its still not working move the entire my-website project folder to a location that is not managed by OneDrive (e.g., C:\dev\my-website) and re-run pnpm install. Understandably this could cause issues and might end up needing a lot of work to fix.

- Try a Different Command: Change the dev script from next dev --turbo to next dev.

body:
Hey everyone — I ran into this exact issue while building a Next.js project using Turbopack + Tailwind + TypeScript + App Router, and after a lot of debugging I think I’ve nailed down what’s going on.

💡 TL;DR

The error

Error [TurbopackInternalError]: Failed to write page endpoint /_error
...
[src]/src/styles/globals.css [app-client] (css)
...
timeout while receiving message from process


is caused by Turbopack’s internal CSS/PostCSS pipeline timing out when Tailwind’s @tailwind imports are processed inside globals.css, especially under GitHub Actions or CI environments.

Locally it works fine, but in CI, limited resources + process message passing cause Turbopack’s CSS transform to hang — leading to that “failed to write page endpoint” error.

🧩 Why it happens

Turbopack runs CSS transformations (like Tailwind + PostCSS) in subprocesses.

In some CI builds (especially with Docker or constrained environments), those subprocesses fail to respond in time, causing Turbopack to throw an internal timeout.

The stack trace almost always points to:

[project]/src/styles/globals.css [app-client] (css)
failed to receive message
timeout while receiving message from process
deadline has elapsed


Removing @tailwind from globals.css or disabling Turbopack entirely usually makes it build again — confirming Tailwind + Turbopack is the trigger.

🛠️ Workarounds / Fixes
✅ 1. Disable Turbopack in CI only

Use Webpack for CI builds (more stable for Tailwind).
In your next.config.js:

const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true' || process.env.GITHUB_ACTIONS === 'true';

const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    turbo: !isCI, // Disable Turbopack in GitHub Actions
  },
};

module.exports = nextConfig;


This keeps Turbopack for local dev (super fast ⚡) and uses Webpack in CI (more reliable 🧱).

✅ 2. Temporarily comment out Tailwind imports

As a diagnostic step:

/* globals.css */

/* Comment out temporarily to verify build passes */
// @tailwind base;
// @tailwind components;
// @tailwind utilities;


If your build passes afterward → the issue is confirmed in the CSS pipeline.

✅ 3. Simplify your PostCSS setup

Make sure postcss.config.js only includes essential plugins:

module.exports = {
  plugins: {
    tailwindcss: {},
    autoprefixer: {},
  },
};


Remove experimental or custom PostCSS plugins.

✅ 4. Create a minimal reproduction repo

This helps the Next.js/Turbopack team fix it upstream:

New Next.js app (npx create-next-app@latest)

Add Tailwind

Enable Turbopack

Push to GitHub Actions → observe the error

Once confirmed, link your minimal repo in the discussion — maintainers really appreciate that!

📚 References

[Next.js Discussion #84495 — “Turbopack failing on GitHub Actions (Tailwind CSS issue)”](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/84495?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

[Turbopack Internal Error reports (Vercel Discussions)](https://github.com/vercel/turbo/issues)

Related CSS parse timeout traces seen on GitHub Actions with Tailwind

✅ Conclusion

If you can build locally but GitHub Actions fails with “Failed to write page endpoint /_error” — it’s almost certainly this Tailwind + Turbopack timeout bug.

Quickest fix:
Disable Turbopack in CI (experimental.turbo = false) until a patch is released.

After that, your builds will pass again 🚀

🧠 Bonus Tip (for maintainers & contributors)

This issue can likely be resolved by increasing inter-process message timeouts or optimizing PostCSS handling inside Turbopack’s CSS pipeline.

That’s it — hope it helps others hitting this weird CI-only Turbopack timeout.
If this fixed your issue, please mark it as Accepted Answer ✅ so others can find it easily!

body:
Hi! This is a common issue with Next.js standalone mode. Here are a few things to check:

## Possible Causes

1. **Cold Start Issue**
   - First request always takes longer due to server initialization
   - Next.js needs to compile and cache the initial pages

2. **Windows Server Specifics**
   - Make sure Node.js has proper permissions
   - Check if Windows Defender is scanning the files on first run

## Solutions

Try adding these to your `next.config.js`:

  ```js
  module.exports = {
    experimental: {
      optimizeCss: true,
      optimizePackageImports: ['your-packages']
    },
    // Warm up the server
    onDemandEntries: {
      maxInactiveAge: 60 * 1000,
      pagesBufferLength: 5,
    }
  }
```

Also, you can implement a health check endpoint that keeps the server warm.

body:
When you have nested `"use cache"` directives in Next.js 15, each cache layer works independently with its own tags and scope.

  In your example:
  1. **Outer cache** (`getTodos` with `cacheTag("todos-${userId}")`) - caches the entire result
  2. **Inner caches** (`getTodo`, `getTodoStats` with `cacheTag("todo-${todoId}")`) - cache individual queries

**How it works:**

  - If the outer cache is fresh, Next.js returns it immediately without calling the inner functions
  - If the outer cache is stale but inner caches are fresh, inner functions return cached data
  - When you call `revalidatePath()` or `revalidateTag()`, only the matching cache layers are invalidated

**Your scenario with `revalidatePath` on createTodo/updateTodo:**

- If you only use `revalidatePath()`, it will invalidate route-level caches
- To invalidate specific todo items, use `revalidateTag("todo-${todoId}")`
- To invalidate the user's entire todo list, use `revalidateTag("todos-${userId}")`

This granular approach is actually powerful for performance - you can update just one todo without invalidating the entire list!

author: onarbf

body:
Yes, exactly! If you `revalidateTag('todo-${todoId}')` but don't revalidate the outer cache, `getTodos` will return stale data.

  **Example scenario:**
  1. `getTodos()` caches the list: `[{id: 1, title: "Buy milk"}, {id: 2, title: "Clean"}]`
  2. You update todo with id 1, changing title to "Buy eggs"
  3. You call `revalidateTag('todo-1')`
  4. Now `getTodo(1)` returns fresh data: `{id: 1, title: "Buy eggs"}` 
  5. But `getTodos()` still returns the old cached list with "Buy milk" 

  **Solution:**
  When you mutate a todo, you need to revalidate both:
  ```javascript
  revalidateTag('todo-1')      // Revalidate individual todo
  revalidateTag('todos-list')  // Revalidate the list
```
  Or use revalidatePath() which invalidates all caches in that path:
  ```javascript
  revalidatePath('/todos')  // Simpler, invalidates everything
   ```
  The trade-off: granular tags give you precise control but require careful management. revalidatePath is simpler but less selective.

body:
The ~110kB difference you're seeing is likely coming from one of these sources:

**Most common causes:**

1. **Vercel Analytics/Speed Insights** - If enabled in your project settings, these add significant JS to the bundle (~45-60kB combined)
2. **Environment-specific code** - Different `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` env vars between local and Vercel can cause different code paths to be bundled
3. **Source maps** - Check if Vercel is including source maps in production (shouldn't, but worth checking)

**Quick fixes to try:**
1. Disable Vercel Analytics/Speed Insights temporarily in your project settings to see if that's the culprit
2. Make sure your local build uses the same env vars as Vercel: `NEXT_PUBLIC_VERCEL_ENV=production npm run build`
3. Check your `next.config.js` for any production-only configurations

**To debug further:**
Run this locally and compare with Vercel's build output:
```bash
NODE_ENV=production npm run build
```

The bundle analyzer can also help identify what's adding the extra weight:
```bash
npm install @next/bundle-analyzer
```

Can you share your next.config.js? That would help pinpoint the issue.

body:
No worries. Case sensitivity matters.

Change this:

```jsx
src="/images/electrical/luminary-drive.png"
```

To:

```jsx
src="/images/electrical/Luminary-Drive.png"
```

To clarify on what's happened here:

> - Windows file system treats file and directory names as case-insensitive. FOO.txt and foo.txt will be treated as equivalent files.
> - Linux file system treats file and directory names as case-sensitive. FOO.txt and foo.txt will be treated as distinct files.

You are likely developing on Windows, so the image works fine, even though you are referring to it in all lowercase. When you deploy, the environment used is Linux, and now the all lowercase name points at a different file.

This error usually appears when Turbopack can’t properly detect your Next.js version or when your build files are out of sync.

Turbopack Error: Failed to write app endpoint /page.

Why it happen ?

The next package might not be installed correctly (or corrupted in node_modules).

The package.json might show an invalid Next.js version (0.0.0 or missing entirely).

Cached build files in .next are mismatched with your current setup.


 Fix Steps :

Install the correct Next.js version
Run this to ensure you have a valid version:

npm install next@latest react react-dom


Clean your environment
Remove old build and dependency files:

rm -rf .next node_modules
npm install


Check your package.json
Make sure it includes real version numbers (not 0.0.0):

"dependencies": {
  "next": "15.0.3",
  "react": "^18.3.1",
  "react-dom": "^18.3.1"
}


Restart the dev server

npm run dev

Extra Tips

If you’re using a canary or experimental build, pin a stable version:

npm install next@15.0.3


Also, make sure your Node.js version is up to date (preferably ≥ v18).

You can read more in the official docs: Next.js Turbopack Documentation

Hope this helps!

body:
For runtime configurations, this is our current setup:

- `.env.development` for development env
- `.env.<dev|staging|prod>` for deployed envs
- `.env.production` contains only env-agnostic properties if they're strictly required at build time

We build in `standalone` mode, then in the container we run using something like
```sh
dotenvx run --env-file=.env.<dev|staging|prod> -- node server.js
```

Then, in the `_app.tsx` `getInitialProps`, if it's a server-side run, we add an `env` object to the `pageProps` where we add everything in the server's env that starts with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. In the browser, we access env from the page props.

Of course this only works with SSR. Some optimizations can be made to only add the env to the page props on the first page load and skip it for navigation.

You can’t set cookies directly from Server Components in Next.js 15.5 because of React’s streaming — the response headers are already sent before cookies().set() runs.
You need to handle cookies in a Route Handler or Middleware, where Next.js still controls the response. For example, put your token logic inside app/api/auth/route.js or use middleware.js to refresh tokens. That’s the only reliable way to set or update cookies server-side in 15.5.

body:
This error usually means Turbopack can’t locate the Next.js package in your project — it’s often related to missing dependencies or an invalid project root.

Try these steps:

1. Make sure `next `is properly installed in your project:

`npm install next react react-dom`


2. Check that your `package.json` includes:

```
"dependencies": {
  "next": "latest",
  "react": "latest",
  "react-dom": "latest"
}
```


3. If you’re running Turbopack manually, make sure you’re inside the project root (where `package.json` is located).

4. Clear caches and rebuild:

```
rm -rf .next node_modules
npm install
npm run dev
```


5. If it still shows the same error, try using the latest Next.js Canary version — this issue happens on some early Turbopack builds:

`npm install next@canary`


It’s likely a bug in older Turbopack versions that fail to detect the Next.js package correctly. Updating usually fixes it.

body:
This error typically indicates that Turbopack cannot resolve the Next.js package within the current project context. It’s often caused by incorrect project structure, missing dependencies, or internal inconsistencies between Turbopack and Next.js versions.

Technical Explanation

Turbopack attempts to locate the Next.js package using a traversal of the project’s dependency tree (starting from the working directory). If `next `is not found within `node_modules`, or if it’s installed globally or hoisted incorrectly (e.g. in monorepo setups), the resolution fails with this error.
Additionally, some early internal Turbopack builds (like `db56d775`) may have incomplete logic for resolving Next.js in custom or experimental setups, leading to false negatives.

Steps to Resolve

1. Verify local installation

`npm ls next`


If it shows` (empty)` or `missing`, reinstall it:

`npm install next react react-dom`


2. Ensure correct project root
Run Turbopack or `next dev --turbo` from the same directory where your `package.json` resides.
Incorrect working directories often cause this issue.

3. Clear caches and rebuild

```
rm -rf .next node_modules
npm install
npm run dev
```


4. Check your package manager configuration

- If you’re using pnpm, make sure `node-linker=hoisted` in` .npmrc.`

- For monorepos, ensure `next `is installed in the same workspace as your app (not only in the root).

5. Upgrade to a stable or canary build
Some older Turbopack snapshots (including `db56d775`) are missing dependency resolution patches.

`npm install next@canary`


6. (Optional) Debug package resolution
Run:

`node -p "require.resolve('next')"`


If this throws an error, the package truly isn’t resolvable from your current working directory.

body:
> 1)is updateTag apply to unstable_cache and fetch with cache?

AFAIK, yes, but moving forward, the idea is to use `use cache` instead of `unstable_cache`

> 2)has revalidateTag for unstable_cache and fetch with cache old semantic, or new semantic?

Err, I am not sure I understand, but the function behaves as described, regardless of the implementation detail - in other words, the function interacts with the cache, rather than with the mechanism to store things in the cache.

As far as I know:

- stale: NOT used for data cache - this is primarily for client-side Router Cache duration
- revalidate: Time until the entry becomes stale and triggers background revalidation (SWR semantics)
- expire: Maximum lifetime of cached entry. After this, the entry is completely invalid and requires blocking revalidation

> What mean has additional cache profile in revalidateTag, if data always refresh right in place?

The profile's expire time is the window of time that stale data is allowed to be served. One that voids, one should block until fresh data is available. If the data finishes refresh between two calls, the second call is now seeing fresh data, and the first call got non-blocking stale data. If the expire time had voided after the first call, and the refresh did not finish, the second call would wait for that to complete.

What do you mean here? `I think expire doesn't apply to render function.`
author: icyJoseph

body:
Both revalidateTag() and updateTag() invalidate cache entries for the given tag, but the key difference is when the data refetch happens.

revalidateTag(tag) only marks the data as stale — the refetch and rerender happen on the next navigation or refresh.

updateTag(tag) immediately triggers a client-side refetch of all data using that tag and rerenders the current route right away.

So:

revalidateTag = “invalidate now, update later.”

updateTag = “invalidate and update now.”

body:
> "With Cache Components enabled, Next.js treats all routes as dynamic by default."

What happens here is that PPR walks your route collecting static parts of the page, and dynamic data that is `use cache`'d, to render a static shell. When it encounters runtime or dynamic data it renders the fallback UI of the suspense boundary wrapping this section, and it also adds it to the static shell.

When a request arrives, it can serve the static shell, and then whatever runtime/dynamic data you had, is sent to the client.

It is a change on how pages are rendered.

> What is exact database query? and fetch

Previously, the stable APIs allow you to opt-in into caching with fetch. However, that's not the only way to get data. Some might use their own client, built on top of the HTTP Node.js module, or file system, etc... further more, configuring fetch was overhead. You can still use it in Cache Components, but you don't have to.

Now you can use put `use cache` where you do your transaction, none of the above matters, cacheTag it, or add a cacheLife, and continue. 

This is good feedback though. I'll make more adjustments to the cache components API reference.

>  cacheLife({ stale: 5, expire: 20, revalidate: 10 }) don't - I got error "Uncached data was accessed outside of Suspense".

I think the https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/blocking-route#short-lived-caches error page is what you are looking for ~ already asked the team internally to maybe link to that section of the docs, in this case, if possible.

I think here the answer is, "just try it", in the sense that:

- if you have a large app where you've been manually memoizing to make the app usable, it is should be OK to have slower build times, so that a wider user base can enjoy a usable app
- in general, having at least the React Compiler linter on is recommended
- Personally, I'd have it on every time

> Are there any functional or performance benefits when using it?

Yes, it has been shown to do memoization devs would not land manually. 

You can also just enable their linter, https://react.dev/blog/2025/10/07/react-compiler-1#migrating-from-eslint-plugin-react-compiler-to-eslint-plugin-react-hooks, to get a sense of your app's code quality

> Is it recommended for production projects, or is SWC alone usually sufficient?

These are different things. The React Compiler optimizes your React code, w/ the aim of reducing re-rendering overhead. SWC takes your code, and transforms it, so that it is correct, smaller, and takes benefit of know tricks for performance at runtime, but nothing React specific. I do believe there's an effort to have the React Compiler in other languages, plugin ecosystems though.

---

I think given your questions, I'd recommend reading a bit more on what SWC is and what the React Compiler actually does.

body:
Turbopack currently doesn’t support resolve.fallback the same way Webpack does — so you can’t directly tell it to replace Node core modules like fs, net, or path with false yet.

The reason is that Turbopack doesn’t polyfill Node.js built-ins for the client bundle at all. It expects client-side code not to import server-only modules.

In other words, while Webpack lets you “silence” imports like fs with:

`config.resolve.fallback = { fs: false, net: false }`


Turbopack’s model is stricter: if a client bundle references a Node-only module, it will error.

✅ Workarounds:

Use dynamic imports guarded by runtime checks:

```
if (typeof window === 'undefined') {
  const fs = await import('fs');
}

```

Move the logic into a Server Component or a server-only utility (server/ folder).

Temporarily disable Turbopack and build with Webpack if you rely on polyfills until feature parity improves.

🧭 Status:
Support for Webpack-style resolve.fallback and module aliasing in Turbopack is still under development — see [next.js#53599](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues/53599)
 for tracking.

body: Hi @svyas-jeavio, you can remove the x-nextjs-cache header by stripping it either in a custom middleware or through your reverse proxy. For example, in Next.js you can add a small middleware that creates a response, deletes the “x-nextjs-cache” header, and then returns it. If you’re deploying behind Nginx, you can also remove this header at the proxy level before sending the response. Currently, Next.js doesn’t provide a built-in configuration option to disable this header directly, so handling it via middleware or at the proxy layer is the recommended approach.

body: You can achieve this by using Incremental Static Regeneration together with on-demand revalidation in Next.js. Essentially, you serve a pre-rendered (cached) version instantly, but can update it the moment your data changes. In the App Router, you can disable automatic time-based invalidation by setting export const revalidate = 0;. Then, whenever your WebSocket detects a database update trigger a revalidation request to your API route. This way the user immediately receives the last cached content while your client-side WebSocket keeps it live and reactive after hydration. Once the data changes, the cache for that route is instantly refreshed for future requests.

body:
It looks like this error happens when Turbopack tries to write the same file twice, usually `app/globals.css.`

Here’s what worked for me:

1. Make sure` globals.css` is only imported once, ideally in your root `app/layout.tsx.`

2. Delete any duplicate routes like

```
app/page.tsx
app/page/index.tsx
```


3. Clear the cache:

`rm -rf .next`

and restart the dev server.

4. If it still happens, try running with Webpack to confirm it’s Turbopack-related:

`NEXT_USE_TURBOPACK=0 npm run dev`


5. (Optional) Update to the latest canary version — this issue has been actively patched in recent builds.

If none of that helps, you can also try adding this in your `next.config.js` to avoid duplicate CSS resolution:

```
experimental: {
  turbo: {
    resolveAlias: {
      './globals.css': false,
    },
  },
},
```


It’s a known conflict between Turbopack’s virtual FS and CSS module resolution — likely fixed soon in the next beta.

body: The rename from middleware.ts to proxy.ts in Next.js 16 Beta is meant to clarify its role at the network boundary, focusing on request routing and proxying rather than traditional app-level middleware logic. body:
This looks like a React version mismatch rather than a Turbopack compiler issue.

Turbopack currently doesn’t suppress runtime React errors — it only stops compiling when a fatal bundling error occurs. That’s why you see the “Invalid hook call” warning but no compilation failure.

Check the following:

- Ensure react and react-dom versions match exactly in your package.json.

- Run npm ls react (or pnpm why react) — make sure there’s only one React instance installed.

- Delete .next/, node_modules/, and lock file → reinstall.

- Avoid symlinks (e.g., local packages) that may pull in a second copy of React.

This behavior (not showing runtime React errors as compilation errors) is known and being tracked while Turbopack error reporting matures.

body: Hi @rmstsd, Next.js automatically manages the ordering of tags inside <head> during build to optimize hydration and preload behavior. It intentionally places <title> and SEO <meta> tags after critical preload links for performance reasons. There’s currently no built-in way to force them to appear first but functionally it doesn’t affect SEO or rendering. If you really need manual control you could inject custom tags using a custom Document (_document.tsx) and place them directly inside the <Head> element  though it’s generally not recommended since Next.js handles this order for optimization
author: haroonmaqbool

body: I'm using App router. Can `_document.tsx` be used?
author: rmstsd

body: _document.tsx is only supported in the Pages Router not the App Router. In the App Router everything inside <head> is handled through the metadata API or the <Head> export from next/head. The tag ordering is managed automatically and can’t be manually rearranged right now even with custom components. If you absolutely need to inject custom tags early you could handle it via a custom server or edge middleware.

body: That delay happens because when a static route is revalidated the cache entry is marked stale, so the next navigation waits for the new payload to be fetched before rendering. You’re basically seeing the re-fetch delay without the loading.tsx fallback. If you want to avoid that blank gap, you can manually trigger a transition state by calling router.refresh() after creating the new prompt, or use revalidateTag instead of revalidatePath so the data layer updates instantly without blocking navigation. That way the page stays static but still refreshes smoothly.

body:
This happens because static routes are pre-rendered and cached, so loading.tsx only appears during client-side transitions when data fetching is pending.

In your case, after calling revalidatePath("/prompts/list"), the new static asset is generated in the background, and the router doesn’t trigger a suspense boundary — hence no loading.tsx appears.

To fix it, you can:

- Use a dynamic fetch (`fetch(..., { cache: 'no-store' })`) or `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` to ensure a proper loading boundary.

- Alternatively, wrap your list component in a `<Suspense>` boundary manually to force the skeleton render during revalidation transitions.

Static routes don’t automatically re-trigger `loading.tsx` after `revalidatePath`, since the cache update happens server-side, not via a client navigation event.

body:
Hi,

> Later, I found that Server Actions cannot run on Server Components, which was expected — but what surprised me was that they also don’t run in parallel. 

There's a whole set of issues arising from concurrently running mutations, that can be controlled by queuing the mutations. Server Actions are primarily for mutations, and it is often the case that concurrent execution is needed when fetching data. 

- https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-server

> Server Functions are designed for mutations that update server-side state; they are not recommended for data fetching. Accordingly, frameworks implementing Server Functions typically process one action at a time and do not have a way to cache the return value.

That being said, two improvements will eventually be added, [source](https://x.com/feedthejim/status/1950232742475813185):

- we will allow actions to be run concurrently if they're not the same
- we will introduce a new API for read-only/GET actions which won't require serial execution at all

Regarding a mechanism to abort Server Actions, I don't have a good answer. We have to start from Server Functions/Actions being a React Server Components feature, not necessarily just a Next.js thing, although they are implemented by the framework. So, this kind of feature would have to be considered from the RSC point of view.

A Server Action is an opinionated way to mutate data, by triggering some server side work. When this model doesn't fit, you have escape hatches provided by Next.js, such as Route Handlers, where you can do this. 

How do we even model this. Most are thinking about just cancelling/ignoring from the client, but we'd also need to make the signal/event available to the server function, so that you can release resources, etc... When fetching data, cancelling at any point is fine, but when mutating data... when the cancellation happens matters a lot 🤔
author: icyJoseph

That said, I still have one **major concern** regarding **how to handle request abortion when performing mutations via Server Actions**.

Currently, I’m exploring how to properly integrate an **AbortController** (or similar mechanism) to cancel ongoing mutations from the client while ensuring that server-side resources are also released correctly.

The challenge is — in the case of mutations, simply ignoring the response on the client isn’t enough. There needs to be a way to **propagate the abort signal to the server function** itself so that it can clean up or stop the work in progress.

I understand that this is a complex topic since cancellation semantics differ between *fetching* and *mutating*, but I’m curious:
👉 **Is there any current recommendation, workaround, or community pattern for safely handling mutation abortion in Server Actions?**

This is the last missing piece I’m trying to reason about — how to gracefully handle server-side cancellations without relying entirely on client-side ignore logic.

body:
Edit:

You may remove it. The prerendering step in Cache Components, takes care of generating a static shell, with fallback UI for dynamic/runtime data. 

For any dynamic data access (fetch, db queries, async file system access), you can either:

- use Suspense fallback UI in the static shell (at request time the data is sent to update the client UI) 
- or cache the results of the operation (include the results of the operation into the UI)

For runtime data (cookies/headers/searchParams), you need to declare a Suspense boundary with fallback UI.

Replacing `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` doesn't really need any other considerations. Just remove it. Unless for some reason, you explicitly wanted to de-opt an otherwise fully static page into render on-demand.

If, you used `force-static` because you wanted to include dynamic data into a static HTML page, then after removing `force-static`, you'd apply the `use cache` directive to the operation fetching this data, and that'd allow Next.js to include it in the static shell.

body:
In Next.js 16, the dynamic route segment config has been replaced by the new static/dynamic rendering model using cache and revalidate.
If you don’t want to enable PPR (Partial Prerendering) for all routes, you can control it per route like this:

```
export const dynamic = 'force-static'; // or 'force-dynamic'
export const revalidate = 0; // disables caching for fully dynamic routes
```

The dynamic config isn’t compatible with experimental.cacheComponents, so you’ll need to remove it and rely on these new route-level exports instead. This gives you the same flexibility without enabling PPR globally.
author: haroonmaqbool

body:
In Next.js 16, the `dynamic `segment config has been deprecated in favor of the new Partial Prerendering (PPR) model.
When `experimental.cacheComponents` is enabled, all routes are expected to follow the new caching and rendering semantics.

There’s currently no per-route replacement for `dynamic `— if you want to exclude certain routes from PPR, the workaround is to disable `cacheComponents `and handle dynamic rendering manually (e.g., via `cache: 'no-store'` or `revalidate: 0`).

The Next.js team is still refining selective opt-out behavior, so finer-grained control may return in a future release.

body:
This difference occurs because `generateStaticParams` directly influences how Next.js builds the route segment’s static vs. dynamic behavior.

When you return` [{ id: "1" }]`, Next.js treats the` [id] `segment as partially static, generating a static route for` id=1` and expecting a 404 for others.
When you return `[{}]`, the empty param causes the segment to be treated as fully dynamic, enabling runtime fallback behavior.

In other words, `generateStaticParams` not only defines which pages are prerendered but also implicitly affects the runtime resolution mode of that route (static, dynamic, or fallback). This is why `product/2` behaves differently between the two cases — one configuration tells Next.js to build statically with no fallback, the other triggers dynamic rendering.

It would definitely help if the docs clarified that an empty object changes the route generation mode, not just the pre-rendered params.

body:
You're absolutely right — returning` []` should ideally behave consistently and not introduce implicit dynamic fallback behavior.

The issue here is that `generateStaticParams `currently acts as both:

1. A build-time hint (what to pre-render).

2. A runtime mode signal (whether the route is treated as static or dynamic).

When you return` []`, the compiler interprets that as “this segment is static but with no generated paths,” and therefore it omits dynamic fallback handling entirely.
When `generateStaticParams `is omitted (or undefined), the segment is considered dynamic and uses runtime resolution.

So technically, `[]` ≠ `undefined `— but the distinction isn’t well documented and feels unintuitive, since both scenarios mean “no paths to pre-render.”

I completely agree that this behavior could be normalized or at least clearly documented. Right now, the implicit dual role of `generateStaticParams `makes it easy to misunderstand its side effects on route behavior.

body:
This is a great proposal — fully agree that NEXT_PRIVATE_DEBUG_CACHE=1 deserves proper documentation.

The log output currently reflects low-level cache operations handled by the FetchCache layer in the Next.js runtime. For example:

get [tag] FETCH true/false indicates whether a cached fetch entry was found and whether a network request was required.

lock get true/false refers to the internal cache stampede prevention lock, which controls concurrent access to regenerating entries during ISR.

set [...] shows when the cache layer writes a new response to disk or memory.

These logs are incredibly helpful for understanding ISR behavior, but without documentation, it’s hard to map them to practical scenarios (e.g., cache HIT vs. MISS vs. background revalidation).

Having an official doc page detailing these signals — possibly linked from the Caching or Debugging sections — would greatly improve developer visibility into how Next.js caching works in production mode.

+1 to this idea — it bridges the gap between framework internals and real-world debugging needs.

body:
Next.js is web framework. It gives you a set of tools, not limited to these, but for your question these are relevant:

- React as UI rendering library
- File system routing
- Webpack and Turbopack bundlers
- Node.js and Edge runtimes
- Development Server
- Build step
- Production Server
- Configuration file
- Router/API handlers and middleware/proxy
- Integrates with React Server Components
- TypeScript support w/ E2E safety

This means that in Next.js you can write React code, including React Server Components in App Router, and Next.js is able to put together all of your code, into modules it can use to serve as described by your File system structure.

To put together all of your code, a process known as transpiling/compiling your React (w/ TypeScript perhaps) code is carried out. The idea is to turn your code into code that Node.js and the browser can understand, and it uses React to generate HTML, and generates other assets needed to serve content on a given route, under the umbrella of Webpack or Turbopack. 

Next.js is able to do this for development or production environments, with minimal differences in behavior. Going from development to production, goes through a Build step, where Next.js is also able to pre-render certain routes.

Once again, to do this, Next.js has configured Webpack or Turbopack to process your input code, to be used by the Next.js server. Webpack and Turbopack are configured to create import graphs, compile, minify, and write to static files, all of your JavaScript, CSS, etc.

I feel like this is enough to prompt more questions? I am interesting in re-using my answer here, but I want it to be derived from genuine questions a developer might have.

author: dufrein

body:
The Next.js server is at the core, a JavaScript file, that node interprets and runs. At build time manifests are generated that strictly define endpoints and assets associated with them. JavaScript, CSS, etc is generated at build time.

At build time, some pages are also `pre-rendered`. At runtime, when a request arrives that pre-rendered result is sent. If the page is dynamic, it'll be rendered `on-demand`. If the page was marked for revalidation, it'll be regenerated in the background. 

In future versions, soon, Next.js will be able to `pre-render static shells of dynamic pages`, to serve content instantly, and stream the dynamic data when it is available. 

So yeah, the Next.js server has some internal logic to look at the incoming request and decide what to do.

This happens because static routes are pre-rendered and cached, so loading.tsx only appears during client-side transitions when data fetching is pending.

In your case, after calling revalidatePath("/prompts/list"), the new static asset is generated in the background, and the router doesn’t trigger a suspense boundary — hence no loading.tsx appears.

To fix it, you can:

Use a dynamic fetch (fetch(..., { cache: 'no-store' })) or export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' to ensure a proper loading boundary.

Alternatively, wrap your list component in a <Suspense> boundary manually to force the skeleton render during revalidation transitions.

Static routes don’t automatically re-trigger loading.tsx after revalidatePath, since the cache update happens server-side, not via a client navigation event.

body:
Isn't this solved with `next/root-params` already? What I do is wrap the imported param function and do the validation there centrally and then use that across the app instead of importing from root-params directly:

```ts
import { locale } from 'next/root-params'
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation'

export async function getLocale(): Promise<string> {
  const resolved = await locale()
  if (!['en', 'de'].includes(resolved)) {
    notFound()
  }
  return resolved;
}
```

If the validation is expensive for whatever reason (maybe you have to go the database or a remote service), you can just cache it.

To me this is far more flexible than rigid exports like `dynamicParams`.

I'm including an explainer about root-params for people that don't know about them, because they are still undocumented:

# What is next/root-params ??

With a layout like the following:

- src
  - app
    - proxy.ts
    - [tenant] 
      - [locale]
        - layout.tsx
        - page.tsx
        - (...)

You can just do:

```ts
import { tenant, locale } from 'next/root-params'
```

These are magically created functions that you need to await:

```ts
const resolvedLocale = await locale()
const resolvedTenant = await tenant()
```

and they are available anywhere in the app from that path downwards (no `Suspense` boundary is required). Very handy.

There are two prerequisites though:

- The root `layout.tsx` MUST be at that level. You can still have other root layouts, `root-params` will export all discovered params but only resolve those that belong to the respective path.
- To avoid turning pages to dynamic, and thus requiring Suspense boundaries, you need to export `generateStaticParams` that returns *at least* one value for each root param (you don't have to return all possible values, Next.js will ISR the rest).

Example:

```ts
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  return locales.map((locale) => ({ locale, tenant: 'knownTenantId' }));
}
```

> [!WARNING]  
> If you do the above, and if your routes are fully or partially static, Next.js will literally generate separate ISR cache entries for *each* root param combination. This might balloon disk usage (or external cache if you're using an adapter). Scaling and cost planning can be a challenge for some kinds of apps.

body:
Hi @girishcx07 👋

Short answer: You can deploy a single Next.js app from a Turborepo without the whole monorepo, but you must (1) build with output: 'standalone' and a correct outputFileTracingRoot (the workspace root), and (2) run the generated server from .next/standalone without reinstalling packages or using a custom server.js that calls require('next').
If you need a fully pruned set of sources/deps, use turbo prune.

✅ Correct build settings (monorepo)
// apps/evm/next.config.mjs
import path from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";
const __filename = fileURLToPath(import.meta.url);
const __dirname = path.dirname(__filename);

export default /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ ({
  output: "standalone",
  // IMPORTANT: point to the monorepo root so file tracing can pull workspace deps
  outputFileTracingRoot: path.join(__dirname, "../../"), // adjust depth to your root
  transpilePackages: ["@workspace/ui", "@workspace/common-ui", "@workspace/orpc"],
  experimental: { /* your flags */ },
});


outputFileTracingRoot must be the repo root, not the app dir, so Next can copy anything your app imports from @workspace/* into .next/standalone/node_modules.

🚀 Deploy steps (no full monorepo)

On CI/build machine (inside apps/evm):

pnpm build     # produces .next/standalone and .next/static


Copy to the server (only what you need):

apps/evm/.next/standalone/
apps/evm/.next/static/
apps/evm/public/
apps/evm/.env   # if used


On the server:

 Do NOT run "pnpm install" here; .next/standalone already contains the traced node_modules.
cd /deploy/evm/.next/standalone
NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 node server.js


Use the generated .next/standalone/server.js. If you run your own custom server.js that calls require('next'), you’ll hit Cannot find module 'next'—standalone doesn’t need next at runtime.

🧩 Why you saw Cannot find module 'next'

Moved the folder then re-installed: running pnpm install --prod inside .next/standalone can break the traced node_modules. Don’t install there.

Custom server: any require('next') or import from next/dist/* bypasses standalone. Use the generated server.js.

Tracing root: if outputFileTracingRoot wasn’t the monorepo root, Next couldn’t copy @workspace/* deps, so the standalone folder referenced packages that weren’t included.

🧵 If you want an even smaller artifact (sources pruned)

Use turbo prune to produce the minimal subset for apps/evm, then build/deploy that subset:

 from repo root
turbo prune --scope=apps/evm --docker out
cd out
pnpm install --prod
pnpm --filter apps/evm build
 deploy out/apps/evm/.next/standalone + .next/static + public


This keeps only the transitive deps needed by apps/evm.

rmdir /S /Q .next
yarn dev   && rem or: npm run dev / pnpm dev

// next.config.js
module.exports = {

body:
Are you self-hosting? And in full control of this app deploys and such? 

---

Otherwise...

If we take a step back, maybe this take:

> cache the request externally using something like Redis
> increases stack complexity, not ideal
> adds some overhead

Is kind of the way to go? Fill the key value look up Db with path -> type associations and use that to route. Yes it is an extra layer, and adds overhead, but it'll get the job done, and be predictable, easy to debug and likely maintain too. 

As long as the latency of doing the look up is very low, this should be fine. 

A less optimal solution would be to try and rely on the fetch cache layer, again, this kind of depends on how much control you have over the deployment, let's assume there's just one deployment, then you could handle all requests in a Route Handler, fetch with cache, so that the response is saved to the data cache, and if the content turns out to be a HTML, proxy to a server component page, and stream that back to the client. 

You'd need to hide that server component page from direct access but it'd get the job done. The latency bulk would be in the one-maybe-two HTTP round trips (client -> route handler -> (possibly) to page -> route handler -> client). Since we relied on the fetch data cache, the page round trip would just read from there and start streaming the response back to the route handler, which in turn forwards that to the client.

That said, I’d like to highlight that the lack of support for cross-module references is a significant limitation for teams using CSS Modules at scale.

Being unable to reference class names across components makes it much harder to build consistent, decoupled, modular styling systems without falling back to :global CSS or workaround with element style and CSS variables.

body: Hi @owjs3901, turbopack runs each loader in its own worker process to enable parallel execution, which means that global variables and shared memory cannot be directly accessed across different loaders. This process isolation is intentional for performance and stability but prevents sharing in-memory state between loaders. If you need to persist or share data, the recommended approach is to use an external store such as a temporary file, a JSON cache, or a lightweight in-memory database like Redis to coordinate data between processes. However, if your goal is simply to avoid parallelization for debugging or deterministic builds, you can disable Turbopack’s parallel loader by setting the environment variable TURBOPACK_PARALLEL=0. This ensures that all loaders run in a single process. At the moment, Turbopack doesn’t provide an API to share JavaScript memory objects directly between loaders, so using an external synchronization layer or single-process mode is the most reliable solution.

body:
Hey @owjs3901, thanks for writing a PR, but we can't accept this for a few reasons:
- Even if the loader execution is limited to a single CPU, the process pool is ephemeral, and we may choose to spin down the worker at some later point, so it doesn't guarantee your global state will actually be retained.
- Turbopack's experimental filesystem cache means that loader execution may be persisted to disk across executions of `next dev` or `next build`, so this won't work as expected. We want to make the filesystem cache default in a future release.
- Global state in a webpack loader is a huge footgun. It's very easy to get it wrong and break caching. We know this from experience because our Babel loader does some custom hand-rolled caching of configuration objects, and we've run into serious bugs with it.
- Parallelizing loader execution is important for keeping Turbopack fast. People will inevitably blame this on us, rather than the plugin that's disabling parallelism.

We do recognize that there is a use-case for reusing work across loader invocations. We have a similar problem with Tailwind, where each worker process ends up having to rescan the filesystem for used classnames because we don't have an API for Tailwind to do that once and re-use the information.

We intend to produce some proper API for this kind of problem. That might be tailored towards Tailwind's usecase, but whatever solution we make will be usable by other tools. We do not currently have any timeline for this, as we need to do a lot of exploratory work first.

In my case, sharing data between loaders is essential for the project I’m working on — a zero-runtime CSS-in-JS library called Devup UI.(https://devup-ui.com)

This is a common issue when upgrading to Next.js 16.0.0 with Turbopack. The error occurs because of corrupted build files and cache conflicts. Here's how to fix it: ## Solution 1: Complete Clean and Rebuild ```bash # Remove all build artifacts and cache rm -rf .next rm -rf node_modules rm -rf .turbo rm package-lock.json # Reinstall dependencies npm install # Try running with webpack first (more stable) npm run dev -- --no-turbo ``` ## Solution 2: If you want to use Turbopack After the clean rebuild above: ```bash npm run dev ``` ## Solution 3: Check for Dynamic Import Issues The "expected chunkable module for async reference" error often relates to dynamic imports. Make sure your dynamic imports are properly structured: ```javascript // ✅ Correct const Component = dynamic(() => import('./Component'), { loading: () =>

Loading...

}) // ❌ Avoid const Component = dynamic(() => import('./Component')) ``` ## Solution 4: Update Node.js Version Make sure you're using Node.js 18.x or 20.x: ```bash node --version ``` ## Additional Notes - Next.js 16.0.0 is still in beta, so some Turbopack issues are expected - Consider staying on Next.js 15.x for production until 16.x is stable - The ENOENT errors you're seeing are related to the build manifest files not being generated properly Try Solution 1 first - it should resolve both the Turbopack error and the ENOENT issues. Let me know if you need further assistance!

This error occurs because Turbopack is trying to read the `/src/app` directory as if it were a file. The error `reading file /home/user/Desktop/pkgs/template/src/app - Is a directory (os error 21)` indicates a file system structure issue. ## Solution 1: Check Your App Directory Structure Make sure your `src/app` directory has the correct Next.js App Router structure: src/app/ ├── page.tsx (or page.js) - This is required! ├── layout.tsx (or layout.js) - This is required! └── globals.css (if using global styles) ## Solution 2: Create Missing Required Files If you're missing the required files, create them: ```bash # Create the required page file touch src/app/page.tsx # Create the required layout file touch src/app/layout.tsx ``` ## Solution 3: Add Basic Content to Required Files **src/app/page.tsx:** ```tsx export default function Home() { return (

Hello World

) } ``` **src/app/layout.tsx:** ```tsx export default function RootLayout({ children, }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { return ( {children} ) } ``` ## Solution 4: Clear Cache and Rebuild ```bash rm -rf .next rm -rf .turbo npm run dev ``` ## Solution 5: Check for Conflicting Files Make sure you don't have both `pages/` and `app/` directories in your project, as this can cause conflicts. ## Solution 6: Use Webpack Temporarily If the issue persists: ```bash npm run dev -- --no-turbo ``` The main issue is that Next.js App Router requires specific files (`page.tsx` and `layout.tsx`) in the `app` directory. Without these, Turbopack can't properly process the directory structure. Let me know if you need help with the specific file structure!

The error suggests that `update-popup` is a directory but Turbopack expects a file. You need to either:

```bash
# Create the missing page file

**Option B: Rename the directory if it's not meant to be a route**
```bash

```

## Solution 3: Clear Cache and Rebuild
```bash
rm -rf .next
rm -rf .turbo
npm run dev
```

Make sure you don't have conflicting route structures. The error mentions both `/(private)/promotions/page` and `/(popup)/promotions/update-popup` - ensure these don't conflict.

## Solution 5: Use Webpack Temporarily
If the issue persists, run with webpack instead of Turbopack:
```bash
npm run dev -- --no-turbo
```

This error is related to Turbopack’s CSS asset deserialization during build — not a problem with your `globals.css` or Tailwind configuration itself.

---

### 🧩 What’s happening
In this stack trace:
failed to deserialize message
invalid type: null, expected a string

csharp
Копировать код
Turbopack is trying to parse a message object from its internal CSS transformation pipeline (involving PostCSS + TailwindCSS).  
However, one of the expected string fields is `null`, which triggers the deserialization panic.

This bug occurs mostly in certain **canary or internal Turbopack builds** (for example `9b25f18e`) and affects projects using global CSS imports under the `app/` directory.

---

### ✅ Temporary Workarounds

1. **Disable Turbopack (use Webpack temporarily)**
   ```js
   // next.config.js
   const nextConfig = {
     experimental: {
       turbo: false,
     },
   };
   module.exports = nextConfig;
Then run:

bash
Копировать код
npm run dev
This lets you continue development while Turbopack’s deserializer issue is being fixed upstream.

Ensure your Tailwind and PostCSS setup is standard
Check that your postcss.config.js and tailwind.config.js are at the project root and properly configured:

js
Копировать код
// postcss.config.js
module.exports = {
  plugins: {
    tailwindcss: {},
    autoprefixer: {},
  },
};
Clear your .next cache

bash
Копировать код
rm -rf .next
npm run dev
(Sometimes old serialized build artifacts trigger this null-type error.)

Downgrade to a stable Next.js version

bash
Копировать код
npm install next@15
Canary builds often include experimental serialization logic changes that may not be backward-compatible.

body:
The problem is that Next.js 16's `reactCompiler: true` flag doesn't currently allow you to control this plugin order, as it manages the compiler internally (and likely runs it first, per the React team's general rule).

To fix this, you must force Next.js to use a custom Babel configuration by removing the `reactCompiler: true` flag, and creating a .babelrc file. This will use Babel for compilation (which is slower than the default SWC-only path) but gives you the control you need.

Create this .babelrc file in your project's root:
```JSON
// .babelrc
{
  "presets": ["next/babel"],
  "plugins": [
    "@lingui/babel-plugin-lingui-macro", // Must be first
    "babel-plugin-react-compiler"        // Runs after Lingui
  ]
}
```

This configuration respects Lingui's requirement and should solve the issue where macros are breaking.

Also, you can check [docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/pages/guides/babel) on how to setup babel.

body:
**cosmetic Vercel warning caused by Next 16’s new proxy/middleware model or an unexpected file-location/name**, not something magically creating a `vercel.json`. Vercel is warning that it couldn’t map a built “page middleware / proxy” output back to a source file with an expected extension, which means any `vercel.json` function mappings (if you had one) wouldn’t get applied. In practice people are seeing this when they add `proxy.ts` (the Next-16 replacement for `middleware.ts`) or when the proxy/middleware isn’t located where the build expects. 

What’s actually happening

* During Vercel’s Next.js build step the platform tries to match compiled serverless function output to the original source file (so it can apply function config). If it cannot find the matching source file (by searching common extensions: `tsx, ts, jsx, js`) it emits that warning. It’s not evidence that a `vercel.json` exists — the message just says that *if* you had function config there, it might not be applied. 
* Next 16 renamed/deprecated `middleware.ts` → `proxy.ts` and changed some expectations about location/exports. If `proxy.ts` is not in the expected place or has an unexpected export shape, the builder can fail to match it. People have seen related warnings/behavior (and sometimes a workaround is renaming back to `middleware.ts`). 

Concrete things to try (ordered by easiest → more invasive)

1. **Make sure `proxy.ts` is in the right place**

   * Put the file at the project root (or `src/` root) — same level as your `app/` (or `pages/`) folder. Next expects a *single* `proxy`/`middleware` file at root/src. If it lives deep inside another folder it may not be discovered/matched. 

2. **Check the export shape**

   * In Next 16, export the `proxy` function (recommended):

     ```ts
     export function proxy(request: Request) { ... }
     ```

     or `export default function proxy(...) {}`. If you still export `middleware` or use an unusual default, try renaming to `proxy`. 

3. **Try the `middleware.ts` fallback (diagnostic)**

   * As a diagnostic: rename `proxy.ts` → `middleware.ts` and redeploy. If the warning disappears, it’s linked to the proxy rename logic/identification in the build path (some platforms/builders still have edge cases). Several users reported this reproduces or temporarily avoids issues. 

4. **Check `pageExtensions` or custom config**

   * If you set custom `pageExtensions` in `next.config.js`, ensure the build still treats the proxy/middleware as a top-level special file — custom extensions can confuse file matching in some edge cases. There are historical issues where custom extensions affected middleware matching. 

5. **Clean caches + redeploy**

   * Locally: stop dev server, delete `.next`, delete `node_modules`, reinstall, build locally: `next build`.
   * On Vercel: trigger a “clear build cache” deploy (the Vercel dashboard has the option). Many build-mismatch warnings go away after a fresh cache because old compiled artifacts can confuse the mapping. (Community recommendations echo this.) 

6. **If you need to avoid the warning for now**

   * If nothing else helps and you can’t find the root cause, you can keep the `proxy.ts` logic but also add a `middleware.ts` wrapper that re-exports/forwards to the same implementation (temporary shim) so the older builder logic finds a source file it recognizes.

When this is a real problem vs cosmetic

* If you don’t have a `vercel.json` with function configuration, this warning is usually cosmetic — your app will still run and the proxy should execute, but Vercel is cautioning you that it couldn’t apply `vercel.json` function config because it couldn’t match the source file. If you *do* rely on function config mapped by source paths, investigate immediately. 

Evidence of this being a current/known area

* Next 16’s migration notes (rename `middleware` → `proxy`) and recent community threads and Vercel posts show multiple people hitting related issues after upgrading to v16 / Turbopack. There are ongoing bug reports/threads; if the steps above don’t help it’s reasonable to open an issue (or link your small repro) with the Next/Vercel teams.

import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry


def make_session(proxy_url=None, proxy_auth=None, timeout=15):
s = requests.Session()
# retries pour les erreurs transitoires
retries = Retry(total=5, backoff_factor=0.5,
status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],

s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries))

s.timeout = timeout
return s

def test_request(session, url):

print("STATUS:", r.status_code)
# diagnostic rapide

except requests.exceptions.SSLError as e:

except requests.exceptions.ProxyError as e:
print("ProxyError:", e)
except requests.exceptions.ConnectTimeout as e:
print("ConnectTimeout:", e)
except requests.exceptions.ReadTimeout as e:

except Exception as e:

if __name__ == "__main__":

body:
My bad, I only looked at the snippet in your OP - 🤦 - when you use `use cache` w/o profile, then the default is used, and that one has revalidate of 15 minutes. After 15 minutes, if a request arrives, it gets served stale content, and then in the background, the content is regenerated. 

`use cache` is meant to allow you to make dynamic data part of the static shell, roughly speaking of course. If your pages are nothing but static content, all of it will be included into the static shell, the end case being that the entire page is just static. 

The build output hints at this, w/ `use cache`:

```console
Route (app)      Revalidate  Expire
┌ ○ /                   15m      1y
```

Without:

```console
Route (app)
┌ ○ /                   
```

It might be the case that you read your content from file system and such (technically dynamic data), you maybe want to use `max` cacheLife 🤔
author: icyJoseph
dninomiya

body:
I think you only needed a very high revalidate right? - the `stale` key is for the client router to keep on re-using data before checking with the server. `revalidate` is the time after which, the next request triggers revalidation (what you are observing) but still serves stale data, the revalidate clock goes back to zero after. 

`expire` is the time since the start or last revalidation, after which the next request, has to block, it has to be higher than revalidate, because the data must first be stale.

body:
The original question was about understanding when a completely static page gets regenerated — meaning, when the .html file itself is updated.

Based on your answer and my own testing, I’ve come to the following understanding:
	•	When "use cache" is not used anywhere → the page is never regenerated
	•	When "use cache" is used → the page is regenerated according to the shortest cache duration

In addition, I’ve noted that it’s possible to create a custom "infinite" option to prevent HTML regeneration even when "use cache" is in use.

Thanks for your support!
author: dninomiya

body: Exactly! Before Cache Components, we'd use this flags to control the route and make sure you stayed within the static optimizations. With Cache Components, it is just code that describes this. If it is nothing but static content, with no async IO or no runtime data is needed, then Next.js can make the entire page part of the static shell for this page. If you eventually add some content that's not static, we won't silently switch the entire route to static, we'll rather require you to handle the non-static content.

body:
I understand now, a little better at least. 

I am adding this to the docs soon, but GET handlers go through the same model as pages in Cache Components. 

Here the access to searchParams, causes the handler to "give up" on build time. Your try catch sees that. If you move the access to search params out of the try/catch then you'd stop seeing this issue. 

**Edit**:

 x-ref: See also https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/87732 for the same error with `request.url`.                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                         
  Two approaches:                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                         
  1. Just ignore it (https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/87732): This error comes from Cache Components attempting to prerender your GET handler at build time. The build succeeds and the route works correctly at runtime. Suppress the logs with

  The build succeeds and the route works at runtime. Suppress the logs with:

```js                                                                              
  // next.config.js                                                                                                                                                      
  experimental: {
    hideLogsAfterAbort: true
  }
```
                                                                                                                                                            
  2. Clean it up (original answer to this discussion): The try-catch intercepts the special bailout error Next.js throws to signal "stop prerendering." - to fix it you may:
 
    - Move searchParams access before the try-catch
    - Or add await connection() from next/server at the top to explicitly opt out of prerendering
    
Next.js throws a special error when you access dynamic data like searchParams - it's how the framework knows to bail out of prerendering. When that throw lands inside a try-catch, it gets swallowed instead of propagating. See https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/route-handlers#with-cache-components for more info.

body:
Our codebase currently has a very large number of pages which have forms in them. These forms have to be empty when navigated to, and `<Activity>` breaks this - the previous form state is shown when the user navigates to a form after previously having submitted it.

In order to enable cache components, we would have to go through each of these forms and manually reset the state on onmount. It would be much easier for us the be able to opt out of this behavior.

If this seems like an non-general issue that is very specific to our codebase, then we completely understand if it’s not something worth addressing at the framework level. We just wanted to share our use case in case others might run into similar issues.

author: ziyak97

body:
It’s been a major pain for us as well, and we eventually had to completely opt out of cacheComponents.

Our applications have hundreds of dedicated form routes, and once they’re implicitly wrapped in <Activity> and no longer unmount on navigation, everything breaks from a UX and logic standpoint. It’s not just form state that gets preserved, all useState values are kept alive, even in places where unmounting has always been the natural reset mechanism.

A concrete example:
We have parallel routes that render a <Dialog> containing a form. The dialog relies on a useEffect that listens to the form action’s success state. On first submission, it shows a success toast and calls router.back().

With cacheComponents enabled, after that first submit, every future navigation to that same parallel route reuses the stale component state. So instead of opening the dialog again, it instantly triggers the success toast and router.back(), making the dialog impossible to access. The component effectively becomes “stuck” in its previous state forever.

Issues like this quickly compound across a large codebase. Retrofitting manual reset logic for hundreds of forms, dialogs, drawers, and components that naturally expect to unmount is simply not realistic.

State preservation on navigation can absolutely be useful, but not as an implicit global behavior that requires every component to suddenly become “Activity-aware”. Right now it feels forced on us in a way that breaks long-established patterns, very similar to the aggressive caching in Next 13.

I really think this needs to be opt-in, or at least offer a clear and granular opt-out at the route/layout level. These features are powerful, but without an escape hatch they can be extremely disruptive to existing, fully correct application logic.
author: JesperCph

body:
Want to anecdotally contribute that persisting state between navigation can undesirably leak user data. I've encountered instances wherein a user on the same tab signs in, performs behaviors that are stateful, logs out, and another user logins during that same local session, leads to the recent user being able to see the previous user's existing state.

With the mechanisms of react activity when cacheComponents are enabled, developers will need to make significant refactors (in breadth) to ensure sensitive state at the very least is reinitialized appropriately under those circumstances.
