body:
For folks running into this, here are a few things to check:

- Next.js 16.0+ separates the dev directory into `.next/dev`, which can make the total size of `.next` larger. While we highly recommend this isolated mode, you can disable it here: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/isolatedDevBuild

- [Next.js 16.1 ships with an experimental bundle analyzer for Turbopack that can analyze client and server bundles](https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-1#nextjs-bundle-analyzer-experimental). You can try this out by upgrading to 16.1 and running `next experimental-analyze`.

- [Cache components](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) (not yet enabled by default) can generate more static rendered files. This is by design.

- [Next.js 16.1 ships with `turbopackFileSystemCacheForDev` enabled by default](https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-1#turbopack-file-system-caching-for-next-dev). The Turbopack cache improves performance, but uses a lot of disk space, and can be disabled here: https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache

- Turbopack is still missing some optimizations that webpack has, though we don't expect it to cause anywhere near a 2x size difference. [Next 16.1 will enable "inner graph tree shaking" for Turbopack](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/85973), and some improvements to side-effect analysis have been staged for 16.2. The side-effect analysis improvements were delayed to 16.2 to give us more time to dogfood and reduce the risk of regressions that a new optimization might introduce.

body:
Hi kyrylolvov,

This error occurs when Next.js cannot locate the Server Action referenced by the client. It typically happens due to one of the following reasons:


1.  Deployment mismatch

   - The request might originate from an older or newer deployment where the Server Action ID does not match the current version.
   - Ensure your client and server are using the same deployment and clear any cached pages or service workers.


2.  Server Action not exported or misconfigured

   - Verify that the Server Action is properly exported in your App Router file.
   - Example:
     export async function myServerAction(data) { ... }


3.  Hot reload or dev cache issues
   - In development, sometimes Server Actions get out of sync due to Fast Refresh or build caching.
   - Restart your dev server and rebuild the app:
     ```
     rm -rf .next
     npm run dev
     ```


4.  Check server logs

   - Look for any errors related to worker initialization or undefined objects in the server console.



- Summary -

The main cause is usually a mismatch between client requests and the current server deployment. Confirm deployments, verify exports, and restart the dev server to resolve the issue.

body:
---

### **My feedback(I hope it solves your problem)**

This behavior is actually expected in **Next.js 15 dev mode**, but it becomes much more noticeable when running inside **Docker**, especially Alpine.

Here’s what’s happening:

---

## ✅ **Why This Happens (Root Cause)**

### **1. Next.js 15 dev server now uses stronger persistent caching**

Next 15 introduced more aggressive dev-mode caching for:

* CSS bundling
* client-side JS transforms
* route-level compilation
* layout/page hydration metadata

This greatly speeds up hot reload **but** it means the browser will often keep older versions of compiled assets unless the dev server signals an invalidation.

In Docker, invalidations often **don’t propagate correctly** because file watchers behave differently inside containerized filesystems.

---

### **2. Alpine Linux + Docker file watching = unreliable**

Alpine uses `musl` + fewer inotify events.
When your local filesystem syncs into the container (e.g., bind mounts), Next.js sometimes **fails to detect file changes**, so it never sends a cache-bust hash to the browser.

That’s why:

* Local machine: everything updates instantly
* Docker + Alpine: browser still loads old JS/CSS until a hard refresh

---

### **3. next.config.js headers DO NOT apply in dev**

Next.js dev server ignores `headers()` caching rules because dev mode uses an internal file server with its own caching system.

So disabling cache in next.config.js cannot fix this.

---

## ✅ **Real Fixes (Official + Community Verified)**

### **✔ 1. Switch to Debian-based Node image (recommended)**

Example:

```Dockerfile
FROM node:20-bullseye
```

This alone fixes 90% of dev caching issues because Debian provides full inotify support.

---

### **✔ 2. Set polling mode for file watching**

In your dev script:

```bash
CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=1 npm run dev
```

Or Dockerfile:

```Dockerfile
ENV CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=true
```

Polling is slower but forces reliable invalidation.

---

### **✔ 3. Force disable browser caching of dev assets**

Add to `next.config.js`:

```js
const nextConfig = {
  devIndicators: {
    buildActivity: false,
  },
  onDemandEntries: {
    maxInactiveAge: 0,
    pagesBufferLength: 1,
  },
};

module.exports = nextConfig;
```

This causes the dev server to **always** recompile fresh assets.

---

### **✔ 4. Don’t use Alpine for Next.js dev environments**

Alpine is fine for production **but not recommended** for development because of poor file-watching behavior.

Even Vercel’s official recommendation is:

> For local development inside Docker, prefer Debian-based Node images instead of Alpine to avoid file invalidation issues.

---

## ❌ What will NOT fix the issue

* Clearing `.next/` → changes nothing in dev mode
* Adding `Cache-Control: no-store` headers → ignored in dev
* Using Webpack instead of Turbopack → same behavior
* Hard reload only temporarily fixes symptoms

---

## ✅ Full Summary

The issue is **not a Next.js 15 bug**, but the combination of:

* Next.js 15's more aggressive dev caching
* Alpine’s broken file watcher behavior
* Docker bind mounts delaying invalidation
* dev mode ignoring next.config.js headers

Switching to a Debian-based Node image or enabling polling mode is the correct fix.

---

body:
I hope my suggestions can help you solve the issue.  It looks like you’re running into an issue with Hot Reload not reflecting CSS/JS changes immediately in Next.js 15 dev mode. This is a known scenario in some setups due to changes in caching behavior and Fast Refresh mechanics.



Here’s a breakdown and some practical steps:

---

 Why this happens:

1. Next.js 15 caching changes

   * By default, some fetch requests and assets may behave differently in dev mode.
   * CSS/JS files might not always reload instantly due to internal caching or module resolution.

2. Fast Refresh / Hot Reload quirks

   * Fast Refresh sometimes doesn’t trigger a full reload for all file types.
   * Style changes (CSS Modules or global CSS) might require a full dev server restart.

3. Browser cache interference

   * Even in dev mode, the browser might serve cached JS/CSS files unless fully cleared.

---



 Recommended solutions:

1. **Clear Next.js cache and restart dev server**

```bash
rm -rf .next
npm run dev
```

This forces Next.js to rebuild everything and ensures updated assets are served.



2. Clear browser cache or use hard reload:

   * In Chrome: `Ctrl+Shift+R` (Windows) / `Cmd+Shift+R` (Mac)
   * Or open DevTools → Network tab → Check “Disable cache”


3. Check your CSS imports:

   * Make sure CSS Modules are imported correctly inside components.
   * Global CSS should only be imported in `layout` or `_app.js`.

4. Optional: Adjust cache behavior in Next.js 15:

   * For dynamic fetch requests:

```js
const res = await fetch('/api/data', { cache: 'no-store' });
```

* This ensures no cached data is used during development.

---



 - Summary -
 
This is mostly a development environment issue, not a production bug. Clearing `.next`, verifying CSS imports, and controlling browser cache usually resolves it.
Hot Reload in Next.js 15 can behave slightly differently, but these steps cover the common scenarios.

---

If the issue persists, providing a minimal reproduction in a GitHub repo can help the community or maintainers give more targeted guidance.

body:
I guess that error message is basically Turbopack saying “I tried to write a file and immediately regretted it.”

Anyway, the usual culprits are pretty boring:

**1. File system permissions being silly**
If Turbopack can’t write the compiled output for `/page`, it might literally not be allowed to.
Common causes:

* Your project folder has weird read-only flags.
* You're running inside WSL and the filesystem is doing its emo phase.
* A process is locking the `.next` or `.turbopack` build files.

**2. The path conflicts with something already there**
If you have:

```
app/page
app/page.ts
app/page.js
app/page/ (a folder)
```

or anything else that would confuse the bundle writer, Turbopack sometimes just gives up.

**3. Corrupted build cache**
Turbopack’s cache breaks faster than my patience.
Try wiping:

```
rm -rf .next
rm -rf node_modules/.cache
```

Then restart your dev server.

**4. An accidental “0.0.0” Next.js version**
The guy used `"next": "0.0.0"`.
That’s not a version. That’s a cry for help.
Your build tooling will absolutely freak out if the actual installed version doesn’t match the lockfile or if something corrupted `node_modules`.

**Fix:** delete `node_modules` and reinstall:

```
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install
```

**5. Experimental Turbopack builds**
He’s using a commit hash Turbopack version. That’s basically running your project on a prototype engine someone welded together at 3 a.m. Wouldn’t be shocked if it’s just broken upstream.

**Fix:** update Next.js and Turbopack to real releases:

```
npm install next@latest
```

Hope this helps.
author: yassine-krichen

body:
Great troubleshooting tips from @yassine-krichen! I'd like to add a few more things to check:

**6. Check Disk Space**
The error "Failed to write" could also indicate insufficient disk space. Make sure you have enough free space on your drive:
```bash
df -h  # On Linux/macOS
```

**7. Antivirus/Security Software**
Some antivirus or security software can block file writes in development directories. Try temporarily disabling it or adding your project folder to the exclusion list.

**8. Run with elevated permissions**
If you're on Windows and running into permission issues, try running your terminal as administrator. On Linux/macOS:
```bash
sudo npm run dev
```
(Though this isn't recommended for regular development)

**9. Check the complete error stack**
Can you share the complete error stack trace? There might be more details after the "Failed to write app endpoint /page" message that could help pinpoint the exact issue.

Also, as mentioned, the `Next.js version: 0.0.0` is definitely suspicious. This typically means your package.json or node_modules are corrupted. A fresh install should fix this.

---

### **My feedback**

This looks extremely promising — especially as AI systems increasingly rely on heuristics, scraping, and partial data to infer site identity. Having an authoritative, self-hosted “source of truth” at `/.well-known/domain-profile.json` feels like a natural evolution, similar to how `security.txt` and `ads.txt` standardized other parts of the web’s metadata layer.

Here are a few thoughts after reviewing the spec and the Next.js package:

#### **1. The Problem is Real, and the Timing Makes Sense**

AI assistants *do* routinely hallucinate or guess domain details, especially for newer or smaller sites. There’s currently no standardized, machine-readable way to declare canonical domain identity data. This fills an obvious gap.

#### **2. The Install/Integration Flow in Next.js Is Excellent**

The zero-config approach with `createAIDomainDataRoute()` is exactly the DX I would expect. Serving the well-known file through the App Router or Pages Router without extra routing config is a big win. The fact that the schema is fully typed is also a huge plus.

#### **3. Mirrors Existing Web Standards (a Good Thing)**

The mental model is immediately familiar:

* **`security.txt`** → security policies
* **`robots.txt`** → crawler rules
* **`ads.txt`** → authorized sellers
* **`domain-profile.json`** → AI-facing canonical domain info

That makes adoption easier.

#### **4. Great That It’s Open & Vendor-Neutral**

The fact that it’s MIT-licensed, self-hosted, and not tied to any SaaS service gives it credibility. No vendor lock-in is the right move for something that aims to be a standard.

#### **5. A Few Early Questions / Suggestions**

* **Extensibility:** Will the spec allow custom fields under a namespaced key, similar to schema.org extensions?
* **Validation:** Are there plans for a CLI or CI validator to help catch schema errors before deployment?
* **Caching:** Any recommendations for caching headers or versioning, especially for domains served through CDNs?
* **AI Adoption Roadmap:** Are there any confirmed or upcoming LLM providers planning to consume this standard? (Even informal commitments would help adoption.)

#### **6. Overall**

The idea solves a real problem, the implementation looks thoughtful, and the DX for Next.js is surprisingly clean. I think a standard like this will become increasingly important as AI systems become a major channel through which users discover and interact with domains.

Would love to keep an eye on the evolution of the spec — especially as more frameworks and CMS plugins are added.

body:
Thank you for the thoughtful feedback! It's exactly the kind of deep engagement we hoped to see. Let me address your questions:

**1. Extensibility & Custom Fields**

Right now, v0.1.1 intentionally disallows additional properties to keep the payload predictable for consumers. The spec does allow the optional `jsonld` field, which can embed full schema.org JSON-LD blocks—this gives you a namespaced way to include extended structured data while keeping the core AIDD fields clean.

For future versions, we're considering a few approaches:
- Namespaced extension fields (e.g., `extensions.vendor-specific`)
- Versioned schema evolution (v0.2, v0.3) with community proposals
- The ability to propose additions through the spec repository

The goal is balancing flexibility with predictability. We're tracking this in our [spec repository](https://github.com/ai-domain-data/spec) and would love input on what extension patterns would be most useful.

**2. Validation & CI**

Yes! We have a CLI (`@ai-domain-data/cli`) that includes validation:

```bash
npm install -g @ai-domain-data/cli
aidd validate --path=./domain-profile.json
```

It's perfect for CI/CD pipelines. You can gate deployments, run it in pre-commit hooks, or add it to your GitHub Actions. The CLI exits with code 0 on success, non-zero on validation failure, so it integrates cleanly with automation.

We also have a [GitHub Action](https://github.com/ai-domain-data/ai-domain-data-validate-action) that validates on every commit. The Next.js package includes built-in validation at runtime, but the CLI is the way to go for pre-deployment checks.

**3. Caching & CDN Recommendations**

Great question. The spec doesn't mandate specific cache headers, but here are our recommendations:

- **Cache-Control**: `public, max-age=3600, s-maxage=3600` (1 hour) is a good default. The data doesn't change frequently, but you want it fresh enough that updates propagate reasonably quickly.
- **Versioning**: The `spec` field in the JSON acts as a version identifier. When you upgrade to a new spec version, update the `spec` URL (e.g., `v0.1` → `v0.2`), which effectively invalidates old cached versions.
- **CDN Considerations**: Most CDNs will cache the `/.well-known/domain-profile.json` endpoint by default. If you're using Vercel, Cloudflare, or similar, the standard cache headers work well. For edge cases where you need immediate updates, you can purge the CDN cache after deploying changes.

The Next.js package sets appropriate cache headers by default, but you can override them if needed.

**4. AI Adoption Roadmap**

This is the million-dollar question, and I'll be transparent: we're still in early days. The standard is new (v0.1.1 just released), and we're focused on building adoption from the publisher side first.

That said, the value proposition is clear:
- LLMs increasingly need authoritative domain data
- The `/.well-known/` pattern is familiar and trusted
- The schema.org alignment makes it easy for AI systems that already process structured data

We're actively reaching out to AI vendors, but adoption on the consumer side will likely follow once there's a critical mass of publishers. That's why we're pushing hard on integrations (Jekyll, Next.js, WordPress) to make it dead simple for sites to adopt.

If you have connections to AI/LLM teams, we'd love introductions. The more early feedback we get from potential consumers, the better we can shape the spec.

**Overall**

Your point about this becoming "increasingly important as AI systems become a major channel" is exactly why we built this. The web needs a standard way to declare canonical identity, and the timing feels right.

We're committed to keeping this open, vendor-neutral, and community-driven. Your feedback helps shape that evolution. If you're interested, we'd love to have you follow along in the [spec repository](https://github.com/ai-domain-data/spec) or even contribute integrations for other frameworks.

Thanks again for taking the time to dig in. This kind of thoughtful engagement is what will make the standard successful.

body:
1. **Why the page is requested during build**
2. **Why the error happens: `Invalid URL: BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic`**

---

# ✅ **Valid Answer**

Next.js is requesting this API **during the build** because your page is currently treated as a **static route**.
In the App Router, if a page has no dynamic signals (cookies, headers, connection, searchParams, revalidate, etc.), then:

➡️ **Next.js prerenders it at build time**
➡️ And your API call runs **during `next build`**, not at request time.

That’s why you see:

```
Collecting page data ...
Generating static pages...
```

This is expected behavior for static server components.

---

# ❌ **Second issue: Invalid URL**

The actual build failure is caused by this:

```ts
api.post("BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic", ...)
```

During build, Webpack treats that as a **relative URL**, so the Node.js Fetch API throws:

```
TypeError: Invalid URL
input: 'BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic'
```

Node’s built-in `fetch()` requires a **full absolute URL** when running at build time.

During dev, this works because you are calling it from the browser.
During build, it fails because the server cannot resolve it.

---

# ✅ **How to fix it (two options)**

## **Option 1 — Make the page dynamic so the request runs *at request time*, not build time**

Add this to the top of your page:

```ts
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";
```

or:

```ts
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
cookies(); // marks the route as dynamic
```

Result:

* The route will NOT be prerendered
* The API call will NOT run during build
* The page loads fresh every request

This is the simplest fix.

---

## **Option 2 — Provide a full absolute URL so prerendering works**

Instead of:

```ts
api.post("BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic")
```

Use:

```ts
api.post(`${process.env.API_BASE_URL}/BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic`)
```

But make sure:

* `API_BASE_URL` exists in `.env`
* And is available during build (NOT client)

Example:

```
API_BASE_URL=https://example.com/api
```

Now static prerendering works because `fetch()` receives a valid absolute URL.

---

# ✔️ Summary

* The page is being requested during build because Next.js is statically prerendering it.
* Your API path is **not a valid absolute URL** during build, so Node’s fetch throws `ERR_INVALID_URL`.
* Fix by either:

  * forcing the page to be dynamic, **or**
  * providing an absolute API URL for build-time fetch.

Both approaches are valid.

---

body:
This is a practical and reliable solution for the Next.js build-time issue you’re encountering.

The error when prerendering `/blog`:

TypeError: Invalid URL
input: 'BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic'

occurs because Next.js executes your `api.post(...)` call during **static prerendering**. Node’s Fetch API at build time requires a full absolute URL. Relative paths like `"BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic"` cannot be resolved, which triggers the error.



 How to fix it:

**Option 1 — Make the page dynamic**
Force the request to run at runtime instead of build time:

```ts
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";
```

Or use dynamic signals such as `cookies`:

```ts
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
cookies();
```


Result:

* The route will not be statically prerendered
* API calls execute on request
* Simplest and recommended for runtime data fetching

**Option 2 — Use a full absolute URL**
Provide the complete URL so prerendering succeeds:

```ts
api.post(`${process.env.API_BASE_URL}/BlogArticleApi_GetListToPageByPublic`);
```


Requirements:

* `API_BASE_URL` exists in `.env`
* Must be accessible at build time



 Summary

The build error happens because Next.js statically prerenders pages without dynamic signals. Node fetch requires absolute URLs during build. Resolving this can be done either by forcing the page to be dynamic or providing an absolute API URL. Both approaches work, but forcing dynamic is often the safer and simpler solution.

body:
You are not missing anything, you have actually discovered a nuance where the documentation simplifies the reality to encourage "correct" architectural patterns, even though the underlying mechanics are more flexible.

Here is the breakdown of why your code works, why the docs say it shouldn't, and the subtle difference between use cache and use cache: remote.

1. Why your code works

The directive 'use cache' creates a function-level cache boundary.

When you put 'use cache' inside getProductPrice, you are telling Next.js: "Treat this function's inputs (arguments) as the cache key and its output as the cache value."

Even though the Parent Component (Page or ProductPrice) is dynamic (due to await connection() or cookies()), the Child Function (getProductPrice) is isolated.

  • The Page: Runs on every request (Dynamic).

  • The Function: Checks the Data Cache. If the key (product-price-123) exists and is fresh, it returns the value without executing the function body.

Therefore, the dynamic nature of the parent does not "infect" the cached function, provided the cached function itself does not try to access dynamic data (like reading headers inside the cached scope).

2. What the Docs mean by "Stops Working"

When the documentation says:

"In a dynamic context: Regular use cache stops working - it won't cache anything"

They are simplifying the behavior of Implicit Caching vs. Explicit Directives.

  • The "Old" World (Standard Fetch): If a page became dynamic (e.g., using cookies()), standard fetch calls without specific cache tags would default to { cache: 'no-store' }. They would stop caching.

  • The "New" World (use cache directive): This directive is powerful. It forces a cache entry into the cache handler regardless of the parent context.

However, the documentation is likely warning you about Static Generation (Build Time).

  • Regular use cache: Ideally runs at build time to prune the code from the runtime bundle (prerendering).

  • Dynamic Context: If the parent is dynamic, use cache cannot run at build time. It forces the caching to happen at Runtime.

In short: Your code works, but it has shifted from "Prerendered Cache" (Build time) to "Just-in-Time Cache" (Runtime), which is exactly what use cache: remote is explicitly designed for.

3. The Difference: use cache vs. use cache: remote

Since both currently seem to do the same thing in a dynamic component (cache at runtime), why does remote exist?

A. Semantics and Guardrails

'use cache: remote' is an explicit signal to the developer and the compiler: "I know this cannot be prerendered. I expect this to hit a remote cache (like Redis) at runtime."

If you use standard 'use cache', Next.js wants to prerender it. If it finds it can't (because it's nested deep in a dynamic tree), it falls back to runtime caching (which is what you are seeing). Using remote removes the ambiguity.

B. Future Optimization

Next.js is moving towards an infrastructure where:

  • use cache: Might be optimized for the edge or static storage (blobs).

  • use cache: remote: Is optimized for high-speed, low-latency key-value stores (like Redis) specifically for shared data that fluctuates frequently.

C. Input Constraints

  • use cache: Extremely strict. It expects purely serializable arguments.

  • use cache: remote: May eventually allow looser constraints or different timeout behaviors suited for request-time fetching.

body:
---
# ✅ **Valid Answer**

The key detail is this:

> **Dynamic APIs (like `cookies()`, `connection()`, `headers()`) don’t *disable* `use cache`.
> They only disable *static deduping and static optimization*.**

This is the part that’s easy to misunderstand.

---

# ✔️ What actually happens under the hood

When you call:

```ts
await connection();
```

or

```ts
await cookies();
```

Next.js marks the route as **dynamic**, meaning:

* No static prerendering
* No static shell in the HTML
* No stale-while-revalidate static caching
* No build-time deduping

But **it does NOT stop the server-side cache handlers** (`use cache`, `cacheTag`, `cacheLife`) from working.

Those APIs are **remote cache APIs**, not **static** cache APIs.

They continue to work because they:

* run at **request time**
* store values inside the **Next.js global runtime cache** (or your remote cache adapter)
* are **independent of static optimization**

---

# ✔️ Why your example still works

Even though the route is dynamic:

```ts
await connection(); // OR await cookies()
```

this block:

```ts
'use cache';
cacheTag(`product-price-${productId}`);
cacheLife({ expire: 50 });
```

creates a **runtime-level memoized cache entry**, not a static one.

So caching still works exactly as expected:

* first request → executes function
* subsequent requests → served from the runtime cache
* expires after the TTL
* works across all users
* works even in dynamic routes
* works during development and production

This is **intended behavior**.

---

# ✔️ What *doesn’t* work in dynamic context

The docs refer specifically to **THIS type of caching**:

### ❌ static deduping of `fetch()`

### ❌ route segment prerender caching

### ❌ static RSC memoization during build

### ❌ auto-suspense static shells

Those optimizations depend on the route being **static**.
Once you call `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `connection()`, those optimizations are disabled.

---

# ✔️ Summary (the short version)

* `use cache` **still works** in dynamic routes — this is expected.
* What *doesn’t* work is **static-level** caching and deduping.
* `use cache`, `cacheTag`, and `cacheLife` use the **remote cache**, which is independent of static behavior.
* That's why your example behaves correctly.

---

Absolutely — and that’s a very fair point.

The current documentation mixes *static caching rules* with *runtime cache handlers*, which can be confusing because developers often assume both share the same constraints.

A couple areas where the docs could be clarified:

### **1. Distinguish static vs. runtime caching more explicitly**

Right now the docs say:

> “In a dynamic context, regular `use cache` stops working.”

But in reality:

* **Static caching & deduping stop working.**
* **Runtime cache handlers (`use cache`, `cacheTag`, `cacheLife`) continue working exactly as intended.**

A small wording change would eliminate a lot of confusion.

### **2. Show a concrete example where `use cache` *fails***

Many people (including OP) will test it and see that it works fine, which makes the current phrasing feel contradictory.

A counter-example showing *why* static caching is disabled when using `cookies()` or `connection()` would make the intention clearer.

### **3. Document the fallback behavior**

If a component becomes dynamic:

* `use cache` falls back to a **pure runtime remote cache**
* It skips build-time optimization
* It still dedupes across users and requests

This fallback is not documented but is critical to understanding why dynamic routes still cache shared data.

---

If the docs included these clarifications, developers would better understand *why* their code works even when the page is dynamic.

Happy to help contribute wording if needed!

Yeah, the statement is correct. Next.js does **not** automatically apply any cache headers to files in `/public`. Those files are basically treated like raw static assets, and unless your hosting layer (Vercel, Cloudflare, Nginx, whatever) adds caching rules, they’ll just be served with default “no-cache or minimal” behavior.

So yes, **if you don’t set `Cache-Control` yourself, your CDN won’t cache them.**
There’s nothing in Next.js that magically turns `/public` into long-lived cached assets.

On Vercel, caching works because Vercel adds the headers for you.
On any other setup, it’s on you.

✔ If you deploy to Vercel

Vercel automatically applies CDN caching to /public assets with long-term immutable caching:

Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable


So on Vercel, they ARE cached automatically, even though Next.js does not set these headers directly.

✔ If you self-host (Node.js server, Docker, Nginx, etc.)

Then you must manually set cache headers, because Next.js does NOT do it for you.

So the real answer is:

Next.js alone → no automatic cache headers

Vercel → adds CDN caching automatically

Self-hosting → must configure caching yourself

# ✅ **Valid Answer **

Your Docker environment is case-sensitive, while your local Windows/Mac filesystem is not.
That means the import:

```ts
import ChartAllUsers from "@/components/charts/ChartAllUsers"
```

will only work **if the folder and file names match exactly**:

* `components/charts/ChartAllUsers.tsx`
  **NOT** `chartAllUsers.tsx`
  **NOT** `Chartallusers.tsx`
  **NOT** `chartallusers.tsx`

On local, these still resolve.
Inside Docker (Linux), they fail.

---

## ✔️ **Steps to Fix**

### **1. Check folder & file name casing**

Verify the exact file path:

```
src/components/charts/ChartAllUsers.tsx
```

If the file is named something like `chartAllUsers.tsx`, rename it:

```bash
git mv chartAllUsers.tsx ChartAllUsers.tsx
```

(Use `git mv` so Git tracks the case change.)

---

### **2. Confirm the Next.js alias is correct**

Your config is correct:

**tsconfig.json**

```json
"paths": {
  "@/*": ["./src/*"]
}
```

**next.config.ts**

```ts
config.resolve.alias['@'] = path.join(__dirname, 'src');
```

No changes needed here.

---

### **3. Rebuild inside Docker**

After fixing casing:

```bash
docker compose build
docker compose up
```

Now Docker (Linux) will correctly resolve the module.

---

## ✔️ **Why it happened**

Local dev (Windows/macOS) = **case-insensitive filesystem**
Docker container (Linux) = **case-sensitive filesystem**

So imports must match *exactly*, including capitalization.

---

Sounds like a Cache Components use case. Have you looked into that? 

When Cache Components is active, the prerender step "stops" at dynamic data (like a fetch or async file read), and requires fallbackUI to generate an static HTML shell. Company details and such could also be made into the static shell with `use cache`, with a cacheLife time that aligns with your "doesn't change regularly". 

I think it'd still make sense to cache the stock data for like 1 second, Next.js still interprets this as a too short cache life, so it requires fallback UI. This would effectively amortize the number of hits going up to source.

body:
There is currently no official support in Next.js for a true “shell + multiple zones” architecture where the shell provides the global layout and each zone renders only the inner page content with seamless client-side navigation.

Multi-zone apps in Next.js are still treated as separate applications, and moving between zones triggers a full page navigation. Each zone must define its own layout because layouts cannot currently be “inherited” or streamed from another zone.

However, there are a few recommended patterns depending on the architecture you want:

1. **Use a single Next.js app with Route Groups**
   This is the recommended pattern today. You can isolate sections like `app/(zoneA)/…` and `app/(zoneB)/…`, while sharing a global `layout.tsx` without duplication.

2. **Use a shared UI package (monorepo)**
   If zones must stay separate apps, you can move the header/footer/sidebar into a shared package and import it in each zone. This removes duplication even though each app renders the layout itself.

3. **Use Microfrontends (Module Federation / Single-spa / Webpack MF)**
   If you need a real “shell” that stays mounted while zones swap content, this requires a microfrontend architecture. It is not something Next.js zones provide today.

4. **Embed zones inside an outer shell using an iframe**
   Not recommended, but sometimes used when strict isolation is required.

**Conclusion**
Next.js does not currently support a single shared layout shell across multi-zones with SPA-like transitions. The recommended approach is either:
- keep everything in one Next.js app and organize it with route groups, or
- extract layouts into a shared package so each zone imports the same UI component.

Hope this helps clarify the current limitations and available approaches.

body:
A few things stand out here.

Since you're already using:

```ts
cache: "force-cache"
next: { tags: [...] }
revalidateTag(...)
```

and the underlying data eventually becomes consistent, this doesn't sound like a simple tag invalidation failure.

My first suspicion would be that you're dealing with **multiple cache layers**, not a single stale fetch.

In App Router, a page can be affected by:

1. Data Cache (`fetch` cache)
2. Full Route Cache (static rendering output)
3. Router Cache on the client

It's possible that `revalidateTag("posts")` is correctly invalidating the Data Cache, but you're still navigating through a previously cached route payload on the client.

A few questions that may help narrow it down:

* Are the pages showing stale data using `generateMetadata()`? If so, is metadata fetched separately from the page data?
* Are you using `unstable_cache()` anywhere?
* Does the stale title appear only after client-side navigation (`<Link />`) or also after a direct URL visit?
* If you call `router.refresh()` after publishing/updating a post, does the inconsistency disappear?

One thing I'd try as a diagnostic step is temporarily adding:

```ts
export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";
```

to one of the affected routes.

I wouldn't keep that in production, but if the issue immediately disappears, you've confirmed that a route-level cache is involved rather than the tag revalidation itself.

Another thing worth checking is whether the list page and the post page are actually sharing the same source of truth. I've seen cases where:

```ts
revalidateTag("posts")
```

invalidates the list query,

but the individual post page is populated through a different fetch, cache wrapper, CMS SDK cache, or `generateMetadata()` fetch that isn't associated with the same tag.

The fact that:

* navigating repeatedly eventually fixes it,
* refreshing twice fixes it,
* and everything converges after some time,

makes me think Router Cache or Full Route Cache is the more likely culprit than `revalidateTag()` itself.

I'd be interested to see:

* your revalidation endpoint,
* the fetch code for both the list and detail page,
* and whether the stale content is in the page body, metadata, or both.

That would help determine which cache layer is actually serving the outdated data.

author: brad-decker

body:
Yes, generateStaticParams (gsP) and dynamic routes, are a bit special. Previously they allowed for a dangerous footgun, namely pages that promised to be static, ISR'able, might have had code paths that trigger cookies or headers, etc, and that'd error out. 

With Cache Components, the framework tries to assert that at least one route can do the render pass safely. The other runtime elements could still trigger a bad code path, but since in most projects routes follow the same structure for all params, one param covers a lot of production cases, not all of course. 

You'd like literally need to say `if (this param) {/* read cookies and return */} else {/* just return a div*/}` in a code path not wrapped by Suspense, which is not very likely to happen, I think anyway, cuz, in this case, you know about that param? I know there can be other checks etc...

Reading params at the top of a Page without suspense but with at least one `gsP` sample, would block on navigation to runtime params not previously visited, but also saves the result to ISR, if there's one (you could redirect and AFAIK, that shouldn't store anything).

This feedback is important, Cache Components is still opt-in for these kind of reasons.

body:
For completeness sake, this means that your rendering pipeline now looks like: 

- `start and complete metadata -> render UI` 

whereas, the streaming metadata optimization allowed it to be:

-  `start metadata generation -> render UI -> if metadata did not complete in step one stream it now`  

So in your case, if your metadata step is slow, it'll impact your UI serving metrics TTFB, etc - keep it fast!

body:
To deploy a React app to Vercel using GitHub, first push your project to a GitHub repository, making sure it includes your usual React files but not the build folder, since Vercel will generate that automatically.
Then go to Vercel, choose “New Project,” and import your GitHub repo; Vercel will recognize that it’s a React app and set the correct defaults. In most cases you don’t need to change anything—the build command (npm run build) and output directory (build/) are filled in automatically—so you can simply click “Deploy” and wait for it to finish.
Make sure your project builds locally before deploying, and add any required environment variables in Vercel’s settings. After that, every GitHub push will automatically trigger a new deployment.

@ellemedit sorry for the confusion here, and the AI answer clearly not having done any checks.

`use cache: private` works only on a browser, the calculation is done server side and sent to the client, which stores it in a client side ephemeral cache. While you can use the other directives, the key difference with `use cache: private` is that it is meant to not store things server side. So yeah, it won't work the way you are trying to use it.

body:
Around runtime prefetching, the feature is still landing a few more bits, but AFAIK, it is not exclusive to private cache. 

Private cache, as I understand it, is something you likely use a couple of times, if at all, in a project. I have an update to the page you linked, and a follow up to private, and then circle back to runtime prefetching as more pieces fall into place. 

Like if you have a `getSession` function from a library, which calls `cookies` from next/headers, you can't really refactor out to use the other directives, so you could perhaps (but not always need to!) use the private cache to store the result in the client, and let Next.js do some optimizations with that information, or just fetch it on demand as needed.

I researched and found that, if you want to fix this issue without waiting for the new version upgrade.
1) npm run dev --webpack
2) Setting > search bar > Type Developer Mode in it > Make these features ON.
By default this feature is ON in mac and Linux, but in windows we have to make it ON.
Why this way work?
Because the new update v16.1.0 came up with new feature i.e turbopack file system caching which use symbolic link(Symlink) to communicate with the OS to work properly and faster. But due to the OFF developer mode it is not able to communicate with OS by created Symlinks, which will throw the error in your terminal which you are seeing currently now. By allowing Developer tools, nextjs is able to create Symlinks and communicate with OS properly which will resolve your problem. If the Developer Mode is OFF then the OS only accept the admin generated Symlinks but by allowing developer mode(ON), Non - Admin can also generate the Symlinks and communicate with OS and OS will also accept the Non-admin Symlinks which make the working perfect and smooth. 
NOTE: You are thinking like if I ON the developer mode, I'm going to face any type of security issue, data breaches in future which is wrong perspectives and misconception.
Developer mode is for the Developer, use it and make your life more better.

body:
I think this one would work too under Turbopack. The thing is that, the type for `ReactCompilerOptions` is very narrow, and doesn't define any of these.

- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/packages/next/src/server/config-shared.ts#L222

So, yeah, it is the contract that is at play here. If you do use `next.config.ts` you''l have to silence type errors.

With my fix, you can get around that, even in Webpack, just do:

```ts
  reactCompiler: true,
  webpack: (config) => {
    config.resolve.alias['react/compiler-runtime'] = require.resolve('react-compiler-runtime')
    return config
  }
```

body: Hey! Love the new bundle analyzer, and love that it allows to view JS data distribution specifically per page (a great DX detail that most other tools miss.) A few points of feedback (I worked with `webpack-bundle-analyzer` & Statoscope quite a bit): - **It’s hard to check if a module is bundled.** Here’s an example of a bundle that has a 30 KB `PnlChart.tsx` module. If you type that name into the filter box, you’ll see nothing – not because the module doesn’t exist, but because it’s too small to be highlighted. Thus, it becomes hard to see if something is actually bundled vs just too small to be seen on the screen: - **It’s hard to see what’s imported sync vs async.** The bundle analysis below shows that the `/` page loads both `moment` and `lodash-es`. But here, `moment` is only imported on demand, via a `next/dynamic` component! The lack of distinction between critical JS and code-split modules makes it hard to see on the glance what needs to be optimized vs doesn’t. - **The `--output` mode could be better.** Running `next experimental-analyze --output` produces a dir with static files that you serve later. This is great and super useful! The advertised use case here is “sharing the analysis with a colleague”, but the way I use HTML reports is different: I usually save a bunch side by side (as I’m optimizing the bundle) to compare the progress and understand what needs to be optimized vs doesn’t. With this use case, I have two wishes for improvements: _1\) It would be great if the report were openable by double-clicking `index.html`._ Right now, you need to `cd` into the dir and run `serve`, and that’s much more friction when you want to quickly peek at an older report. (Ideally, the report would be a single `.html` file with everything bundled into it – like in `webpack-bundle-analyzer` and Statoscope. That would make working with it a breeze.) _2\) It would be great if the report dirs had a timestamp in their name._ Right now, if you run `next experimental-analyze --output`, change something, and then run `next experimental-analyze --output` again, the new report overrides the previous report. This kills the use case of comparing several reports side by side, unless you make manual copies. (Both `webpack-bundle-analyzer` and Statoscope solve this by 1) producing a single HTML file, 2) putting a timestamp into its name, and 3) putting it in the root of the project.)

body:
Hey @vinay-blink 👋

This specific Turbopack crash (`Next.js package not found → get_next_package failed`) almost always means Turbopack can’t find your `next` package in `node_modules`. It hits this when `node_modules/.bin/next` is missing or the `next` dep is broken/malformed.

Happens a lot with:

- pnpm (hard links confuse Turbopack sometimes)
- monorepos where `next` isn’t hoisted
- corrupted node_modules after a bad install
- `next` listed in `devDependencies` but not `dependencies` in some setups

Quick fixes (try in order):

```bash
# 1. Just nuke and reinstall
rm -rf node_modules .next
npm install   # or yarn / pnpm / whatever you use

# 2. If you’re on pnpm, force hoisting for next
# add to .npmrc
node-linker=hoisted

# or just temporarily switch to npm/yarn for next@canary/turbopack
```

I’ve seen this exact stack trace probably 20+ times in the last couple months and 99% of the time it’s fixed by a clean install.

If that doesn’t do it, drop your `package.json` and lockfile name (package-lock/yarn/pnpm-lock) here and I’ll tell you exactly what’s up.

Works after the reinstall? 🚀

body:
Hey @fleizean 👋

Yeah this is a classic NAT loopback / hairpinning problem on Windows Server + IIS. The Next.js node process is resolving `api.example.com` to the public IP, then trying to connect back to itself from the outside, and your firewall/router either blocks it or just times out.

The cleanest and most common fix in this exact setup (IIS + iisnode + multiple subdomains on the same box) is:

### Do BOTH of these:

1. Use a server-only env var for internal calls  
   Keep your public one for the client:
   ```env
   # .env.production
   NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://api.example.com
   INTERNAL_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3001   # or whatever port your backend actually listens on
   ```

   Then in your `myApiService` do:
   ```ts
   const baseURL = typeof window === 'undefined' 
     ? process.env.INTERNAL_API_URL 
     : process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL;
   ```

   This way SSR/fetch on the server always hits localhost directly → instant, no SSL issues, no loopback problem.

2. If for some reason you still want/need to call it via HTTPS internally (not recommended), add the hostname mapping to the server’s hosts file:
   ```
   127.0.0.1 api.example.com
   ```
   But then you’ll hit cert hostname mismatch unless the cert includes `localhost` or you disable verification (don’t do that).

Honestly just go with option 1. Everyone running Next.js + separate API on the same machine (Vercel or not) does it this way. Zero downsides and it works everywhere (dev, Docker, IIS, whatever).

Bonus: you can even keep the port out of the URL and do `http://localhost` — iisnode will still resolve it correctly inside the same box.

I’ve been burned by this exact thing on IISNode years ago — the INTERNAL_ prefix trick fixes it 100% of the time.

Let me know if that works!

Next.js internally syncs to React canary channel/version. Each update is done through an actual PR to Next.js where the React dependencies being consumed are `compiled` and vendored in, they pass all unit and e2e tests and are merged to canary, which then after some time is released, or back-ported into a older versions, whatever necessary.

body:
React Fiber is a reimplementation of React’s core engine, designed to make rendering interruptible, incremental, and prioritized.
Instead of rendering everything in a single synchronous pass, React breaks work into small chunks using a linked-list tree structure called Fiber nodes.
author: 0x-ZeroTrace

body: When setState is called, React creates an update object and places it in the component’s update queue. The scheduler assigns a priority to the update and marks the affected Fiber subtree as dirty. React then enters the render (reconciliation) phase, building a work-in-progress Fiber tree by running beginWork and completeWork on each Fiber. This phase is interruptible. React collects all necessary DOM changes in an effect list. When the render phase completes, React enters the synchronous commit phase, applies DOM mutations, runs layout effects, triggers the browser paint, and finally runs passive effects. At the end, React swaps the new Fiber tree into place, and the UI is updated.

body:
## Answer

Great observations — there are actually **two separate things** to clarify here, and understanding each one makes the behavior fully predictable.

---

### 1. Why is `cssChunking` both "experimental" and enabled by default?

The `experimental` namespace in Next.js does **not** mean "disabled by default" or "not safe for production." It means the **API surface (the config option name and its accepted values) may still change** in a future release without a semver major bump. The underlying chunking logic itself has been battle-tested and is running in production at scale — the `experimental` label is a **stability contract caveat**, not a warning about correctness or readiness.

This is a consistent pattern in Next.js: many features graduate from `experimental.*` to a top-level config option once the API is considered stable. Until then they live under `experimental` even if they are on by default and recommended for production. For `cssChunking: true` specifically, the [docs confirm](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cssChunking):

> For most applications, we recommend `true` as it leads to fewer requests and better performance.

So: ✅ safe for production, ⚠️ API name/values may change in a future version.

---

### 2. Why does your app produce *more* chunks with `cssChunking: true`, not fewer?

Your self-diagnosis is exactly correct. Here's the precise mechanism:

**With `cssChunking: false`:**
Your catch-all route (`[...slug]`) acts as a gravity well for the entire component tree. Because everything routes through it, webpack's `SplitChunksPlugin` sees all the CSS as "shared" across a single entry and collapses it into one large output file (626 KB in your case). You get fewer files, but the payload is monolithic — every page loads all CSS regardless of what it actually uses.

**With `cssChunking: true`:**
Next.js analyzes the **import graph** across all routes, not just the catch-all. It determines which CSS modules are genuinely independent and can be split into separate chunks without risking order-dependent style conflicts. The catch-all's 626 KB blob gets broken apart because most of those CSS modules are **also imported from other routes** — so the chunker splits them out so they can be shared (and cached) across routes rather than re-bundled into one big file per route.

The **chunk count goes up** (28 vs 18), but this is the correct trade-off: smaller, cacheable, route-specific chunks vs fewer but larger monolithic files. The total CSS size being roughly equal confirms the logic is working as designed — it's redistributing, not duplicating.

The side effect you noticed (routes outside the catch-all pulling in CSS they don't need) is a known limitation of the current graph-based heuristic — the chunker has to decide at build time which CSS is "shared," and with a catch-all touching nearly everything, the shared surface is large.

---

### To answer your questions directly:

**Q1: Is it expected that production apps keep `cssChunking` enabled?**

Yes. For most apps, `true` is the right default. The "experimental" label is about API stability, not production readiness.
author: Saobia3i

body:
@simonepizzamiglio You’re right to notice the mixed signals in the docs — it’s a bit confusing when something is marked “experimental” and “not recommended for production,” but also enabled by default.

Here’s the current state of `experimental.cssChunking` in Next.js:

**Why it exists :** 

The idea is to merge CSS output so you don’t end up with dozens of tiny style chunks. In practice, depending on how your app is structured (dynamic routes, CMS‑driven content, lots of layouts), the heuristic can sometimes split more aggressively instead of merging.

**Enabled by default :**

It was turned on by default to reduce requests in common cases, but the team quickly added the option to disable it after reports like yours where chunk counts went up.

**Production guidance :**

It’s safe to ship with it enabled if it improves your bundle in your project. But it’s not guaranteed to help every app, which is why the docs caution against relying on it in production until the heuristics are more stable.

**What to do :**  
  1. Measure in your own app — if enabling produces *more* CSS chunks, you’re better off disabling it.  
  2. If disabling reduces chunk count and improves performance, that’s the recommended path for now.  
  3. Keep an eye on Next.js release notes — the behavior is still being tuned, and future versions may change the default or improve merging logic.

👉  it’s expected that production apps can keep it enabled if it helps, but you should absolutely disable it if you see the opposite effect. The “experimental” label is there because the merging logic isn’t consistent across all project shapes yet.

body:
It looks like you’re getting hit by the same RCE payload scans that are going around right now, even though 14.2 is not in the officially affected range.

The Next.js security advisory says the RSC exploit affects:

- Next 15.x
- Next 16.x
- 14.3 canary builds

So 14.2 shouldn’t be vulnerable to the exploit itself.
But scanners don’t care about the version — they just spray payloads at every public endpoint, and that can still trigger weird runtime errors if your app hits an unexpected code path.

The   `"Cannot read properties of null (reading 'digest')"` error usually means the request crashed somewhere in the RSC or auth/crypto pipeline because the incoming payload is malformed. If your process manager restarts on unhandled rejections, it will look like the “attacks are restarting the server.”

**A few things you can do:**

1. Update within the 14.x line

    Stay on 14.2, but make sure you’re on the latest patch. You get fixes without jumping into 15/16.

2. Put a WAF or rules in front
    Cloudflare / AWS / Vercel Edge Rules can block obviously malicious payloads before they reach Node. This makes a huge difference during exploit waves.

4. Add limits + defensive checks

   Rate-limit anonymous POSTs and enforce body size limits so large payloads don’t reach RSC internals.

5. Stop unhandled promise rejections from crashing the app

    Even adding a simple handler to log instead of crash can stabilize things while you investigate.


```
process.on('unhandledRejection', (err) => {
  console.error('Unhandled rejection:', err);
});
```


6. Monitor the specific endpoint being hit

    If you can log the route, you can sometimes isolate the part of your app that throws when it receives unexpected input.

So in short: your version is not actually vulnerable, but the exploit traffic can still cause crashes if bad inputs hit brittle parts of the runtime. Hardening the edge and tightening error handling usually stops the restarts.

body:
This error usually happens when Turbopack tries to read a folder as if it were a CSS file. In your case, it's trying to open this path:  app/(pages)

But since that’s a directory, Turbopack throws:   “Is a directory (os error 21).”

**Here are two things to check:**

Look inside your app/globals.css (or any CSS file you edited) and make sure you’re not importing the (pages) folder by mistake.
Sometimes something like this appears:

```
@import "./(pages)";
```

If you see anything like that, remove it or point it to an actual .css file.

Try renaming the folder
Turbopack can be sensitive to folder names with parentheses.
Rename:

```
(pages) → pages
```


After that, delete your .next folder and restart:

```
rm -rf .next
npm run dev
```


This usually fixes it.

React 19.2.0 isn’t affected by this CVE. The vulnerability was in Next.js’ RSC and Server Actions handling, not React itself. That logic lives entirely in Next.js’ server runtime.

body:
https://nextjs.org/docs#react-version-handling

When you use App Router, Next.js manages the version of React. In this case, upgrading Next.js to 16.0.7 includes the React patch. 

As you can see here, the least three patches contain the fix: https://github.com/facebook/react/releases for React Flight protocol which handles Server Functions, that patches React version, for example `19.2.1` - While: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/releases/tag/v16.0.7 (and every other release Next.js has done for this CVE) contains the patches for React as well.

You may also upgrade your react and react-dom dependencies too, but in App Router applications, it is Next.js that handles has a vendored/compiled version of React within its source control.

body:
Hi @primeautomation-dev.

This is a combination of WSL networking + project location + config.

### Main issue
`output: "export"` is meant for **static export builds**, not for running the dev server.
When using `next dev`, it can cause unexpected behavior, especially under WSL.

### What to fix

#### 1. Remove `output: "export"` for development
In `next.config.js`, remove:
```js
output: "export"


Use it only when you are doing:
```
next build
next export
```

2. Ignore the `appDir` warning
This warning:
`Unrecognized key(s) in object: 'appDir' at 'experimental'`
means you are on Next.js 14.

`appDir` is no longer needed under `experimental `and should be removed:
```
experimental: {
  // remove appDir
}

```

3. Move the project out of `/mnt/c`
Running Next.js dev server from `/mnt/c` under WSL often causes filesystem and networking issues.

✅ Best practice:
`/home/your-user/projects/my-next-app`

Then reinstall:
```
rm -rf node_modules package-lock.json
npm install
npm run dev
```


4. Use default dev port
Port `5173` is usually associated with Vite.
For Next.js, let it run on the default port:
`http://localhost:3000`
or explicitly:
`npm run dev -- -p 3000`




**### Summary**

`output: "export"` should not be used with `next dev`

Remove deprecated `appDir` config

Avoid running Next.js dev server from `/mnt/c` in WSL

Run the project inside WSL filesystem

After these changes, the dev server should open correctly in the Windows browser

Hope this helps 👍

body:
Next.js (and React in general) doesn’t have a built-in “midroll ads” feature like YouTube. Next is just the web app framework — the “show ads at timestamps while a video plays” behavior has to be implemented by you (or by using a video player / ad SDK that supports it).

You can absolutely build it in a Next app, but it’s not a Next “video feature”.

What you typically do instead:

- Use a video player that gives you playback time events (HTML5 `<video>`, hls.js, Shaka Player, video.js, etc.)
- Define an ad schedule like:
  - at 30s: play ad A
  - at 120s: play ad B
- While the main video plays, listen to `timeupdate` (or a more precise timer), and when you hit a timestamp:
  - pause the main video
  - play an ad video (pre-roll/mid-roll)
  - then resume the main video at the same time

Two common approaches:

1) “Simple custom” (works if you control the ad files)
- pause main video
- swap the `<video src>` to the ad
- after ad ends, swap back and seek to the saved time

2) “Real ads like YouTube” (industry standard)
If you want proper ad behavior (tracking, skipping rules, reporting, ad decisioning), you typically integrate an ad tech SDK:
- Google IMA (VAST/VMAP)
- SSAI/HLS ad insertion platforms
These can handle midroll timing, clickthroughs, metrics, etc., but they’re more complex.

So the answer is:
- Next.js can host/build the UI and logic for this
- but it doesn’t provide it out of the box
- you’ll implement it with a player + timing logic (simple) or an ad SDK (production-grade)

body: Move the cached function to a separate file without "use server" directive. The "use cache" directive does NOT work when used inline inside a file marked with "use server" at the top - the directives are mutually exclusive at file scope level. Create a new file (e.g., `lib/cache.ts`) with "use cache" at the top containing your cached function, then import and use it in your "use server" file.

> Also, I noticed that when I remove cacheTag, it fetches from the cache (The log starts with Cache...) which makes me believe that it works. I just can't seem to figure out why it breaks when I add cacheTag.

Are you perhaps also calling this function elsewhere? Causing a misattribution? 

AFAIK, Cache semantics, including Data Cache (the one fetch uses) are not supported in Proxy/Middleware. Cache components semantics was never going to work in middleware, because that uses only edge runtime. Now that Proxy forces run on nodejs and middleware may run on that runtime too, it is understandable that this confusion would happen. 

I'll do some more investigation though, and likely end up with a docs update.

body:
The thing is that proxy/middleware, were designed initially to be a separate cart. Many Next.js features don't necessarily have a counter part in proxy. 

Such is the case for cache components. 

Your original title, is about whether or not server actions may use cache directives, and for that the answer is **yes**.

Calling a Server Function from proxy/middleware, is as good as just calling a regular async function. Does proxy/middleware allow cache directives? It is not supported at the moment.

Applications using React Server Components with the App Router are affected when running:

- Next.js 13.x, Next.js 14.x stable, Pages Router applications, and the Edge Runtime are not affected.

- 15.0.5
- 15.1.9

body:
This is a well-known and documented Turbopack behavior, not a bug — but the gap is larger than it should be for production builds. Here's what's happening and what you can do about it.

## Why Turbopack Produces Larger Bundles

### 1. Different Chunking Strategy

Turbopack and Webpack use fundamentally different chunking algorithms. Webpack's default chunking with `SplitChunksPlugin` aggressively deduplicates shared modules — a dependency like `react-dropzone` that appears in 10 routes gets hoisted into a single shared chunk. Turbopack currently produces more, smaller chunks per route without the same level of cross-route deduplication, which leads to the same library appearing in multiple bundles.

This is being actively worked on by the Turbopack team — see the [Turbopack roadmap](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/optimizing/bundle-analyzer) and the tracking issue for chunk optimization.

### 2. Dev vs Production Bundle Difference

Are you comparing `next build` (Turbopack) vs `next build --webpack`? Turbopack's **production build** (`next build`) still uses Webpack for the final production bundle as of Next.js 14/15 — Turbopack is primarily used for the **dev server** (`next dev --turbo`).

If you're seeing large bundles from `next build` (no `--turbo` flag), that's actually still Webpack under the hood.

```bash
# Dev server with Turbopack (fast refresh, no production optimization)
next dev --turbo

# Production build - still uses Webpack (as of Next.js 14/15)
next build

# Experimental: full production Turbopack
next build --experimental-turbopack  # Not recommended for production yet
```

### 3. Source Maps and Debug Info in Dev Mode

If you're measuring bundle sizes from the dev server (`next dev --turbo`), you're comparing development builds. Turbopack dev bundles include more debugging metadata, inline source maps, and HMR runtime code that Webpack dev mode handles differently. **Never compare bundle sizes from dev servers** — use production builds only.

## What to Actually Do

### Verify You're Comparing Apples to Apples

```bash
# Correct comparison:
next build              # Webpack production (current default)
# vs
next build --experimental-turbopack  # Turbopack production (experimental)

# Do NOT compare:
next dev --turbo        # vs
next build --webpack    # Different modes!
```

### Analyze What's Actually Large

Use the built-in bundle analyzer:

```bash
ANALYZE=true next build
```

Or via `@next/bundle-analyzer`:

```js
// next.config.js
const withBundleAnalyzer = require('@next/bundle-analyzer')({
  enabled: process.env.ANALYZE === 'true',
})
module.exports = withBundleAnalyzer({})
```

This will show you exactly which modules are being duplicated across chunks and by how much.

### If Using App Router, Check for Client Component Boundaries

Over-broad `'use client'` directives cause large client bundles. Keep server components as server components and only mark the interactive leaf components as `'use client'`.

## Current Status

The Vercel team has acknowledged that Turbopack's production bundle optimization is a known area of active development. For now:
- Use `next dev --turbo` for fast development (this is Turbopack's strength)
- Use the default `next build` (Webpack) for production until Turbopack's production bundling stabilizes
- Track [this GitHub issue](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/issues) for Turbopack production bundle size improvements

In our repository I noticed a big difference in size between webpack and turbopack due to the usage of `zod`. Didn't fully understand until I read this https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/issues/5561#issuecomment-4331467925 from the maintainer. Seems like Turbopack handles the tree-shaking quite different for the way their code is structured.

When I changed `import { z } from "zod"` to `import * as z from "zod"` throughout our codebase it seemed to tree-shake the locales correctly, however I wish we didn't have to do this as some bundlers (including webpack) seem to handle the old import fine out of the box.

The vulnerability originates, as per https://react.dev/blog/2025/12/03/critical-security-vulnerability-in-react-server-components, in react libraries:

> The vulnerability is present in versions 19.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1, and 19.2.0 of:
> 
> [react-server-dom-webpack](https://www.npmjs.com/package/react-server-dom-webpack)
> [react-server-dom-parcel](https://www.npmjs.com/package/react-server-dom-parcel)
> [react-server-dom-turbopack](https://www.npmjs.com/package/react-server-dom-turbopack?activeTab=readme)

In App Router, Next.js manages your React packages for you, https://nextjs.org/docs#react-version-handling, so to patch the vulnerabilities above, a Next.js update is necessary.

- Blog post with disclosure: https://nextjs.org/blog/CVE-2025-66478
- Security advisory: https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-9qr9-h5gf-34mp
- CVE: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2025-55182
- Required Action: https://nextjs.org/blog/CVE-2025-66478#required-action
  - Includes [versions to upgrade to](https://nextjs.org/blog/CVE-2025-66478#fixed-versions) - includes all of the 15 range stable versions, as well as version 16
  - Includes https://www.npmjs.com/package/fix-react2shell-next a CLI to one shot fixes
- We also have various patches for those who need to stay in a canary, https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/86813 but that's likely not your case
- We have a patched canary for those who want to use PPR in canary

Last but not least, Vercel's security bulletin: https://vercel.com/kb/bulletin/react2shell with even more info.

author: lolelu

body: For anyone hitting this **intermittently during static export** (random page each run, fine on Vercel/CI, fails on a loaded dev machine): filed vercel/next.js#95545 with a mechanism analysis and a statistical repro. Short version: `getFlightResponse` memoizes per stream at first touch and reads `workUnitAsyncStorage.getStore()` from whatever async context gets there first; the prerender abort path and stream backpressure-resume both execute outside the `run()` scope, so under CPU load a random page's first touch lands store-less → E696. Workaround that has absorbed every occurrence for us: `experimental: { staticGenerationRetryCount: 3 }`.

body:
One thing I’d strongly consider here is separating raw file ingestion from the rest of the server action flow.

For uploads that matter, I’ve had better results using a dedicated upload endpoint/route, inspecting the file server-side before storage, and only then passing a safe reference/id into the rest of the app. That avoids mixing “transport concerns” with the trust decision.

I built an OSS package for this layer in Node.js called Pompelmi:
https://github.com/pompelmi/pompelmi

It focuses on inspecting untrusted uploads before persistence (content-based checks, MIME/extension mismatch detection, risky archive structure signals, optional YARA/quarantine hooks). Even if the root cause here is a Next regression, that split usually makes the pipeline much easier to reason about.

body:
I realized that cacheHandler can’t be used when cacheComponents: true is enabled. In that case, you need to use cacheHandlers instead, defining both the default handler and the remote one.

What I’m not fully sure about now is whether both approaches can be used together or what the recommended pattern is, especially when running the cache on a self-hosted Redis instance.

Also, when using cacheHandlers with a custom default handler, it seems that revalidatePath no longer works. It looks like only updateTag works, because revalidatePath expects the _N_T_/page tag to exist — and that tag is not stored when using cacheHandlers.

References:

https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/incrementalCacheHandlerPath

https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers
author: ezeparziale

body:
~Gotta update the docs, surprised I missed updating that these are mutually exclusive.~

Yeah, so for soft tags (the implicit route tags like `_N_T_/products` that come from revalidatePath), there are two ways to handle them:

- Your getExpiration(tags) returns the timestamp when those tags were invalidated, and Next.js compares it against the cache entry's timestamp.

- or, you return Infinity from getExpiration, which means the above check is skipped, and then in your get(cacheKey, softTags) method, you check that second softTags argument against your store to see if any were invalidated after the entry was created.

For both approaches the `updateTags` method should somehow store the tags it receives w/ an invalidation timestamp (both hard tags from revalidateTag and soft tags from revalidatePath). 

- Here's a community implementation: https://github.com/mrjasonroy/cache-components-cache-handler/blob/main/packages/cache-handler/src/data-cache/memory.ts that uses a global Map to store cache tag invalidation info.

body:
It's time to drop an update here.

There has been some confusion for `cacheHandler` and `cacheHandlers` usage. One thing we should state clearly is that you can use both.

In the case of OP here, the problem is serialization. As this issue points out: https://github.com/mrjasonroy/cache-components-cache-handler/pull/29

> Next.js 16 stores segmentData as a Map<string, Buffer> and rscData as a Buffer on APP_PAGE cache entries. Plain JSON.stringify converts Maps to {} and loses Buffer identity, so on deserialization segmentData.get() throws

And the solution, as the PR also points out, is to fix the serialization (and deserialization).

> Adds custom jsonReplacer/jsonReviver to the Redis ISR handler that preserve Map and Buffer types through the serialization round-trip

Your code with getServerSideProps is fine if the data changes a lot or you need it fresh on every visit.

Use getStaticProps + getStaticPaths if your posts don’t update often — Next.js will pre-build the pages at build time, so they load super fast.

Quick rule of thumb:
Blog posts, docs, marketing pages → getStaticProps.
User dashboards, real-time stats → getServerSideProps.

body:
Hiyo, I am about to merge an update that fixes that example.

`generateStaticParams` makes it so that the `param` on that page is known at build time, so you can read it without Suspense around it, and prerender can go ahead and generate that page. 

Then, at runtime, the first time a new dynamic params is requested, it render blocks, serves and saves to disk. The next time this param is requested it serves immediately. 

Without at least one sample parameter, (docs for this coming up too) - then there's no way to check what this route does.

IIRC, we are trying to differentiate this, and other errors, so that you'd end up in a more appropriate error page. For example: https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/empty-generate-static-params would've been arguably more helpful.

body:
Yes docs only for now. I've frame it as build-time validation, but I am already thinking of reframing it into more of a way, in which Next.js gives you feedback to help you see where dynamic behavior exists.

It is not so much magic really, but how would one figure out the static shell, other than running the code. You provide a param, so Next.js can make more progress in your route, so more of the page can be added to the prerendered HTML. I think there's also a compounded benefit when you have 2-3 params, but I haven't worked with it beyond the demo state. 

In short, the more params variations you can provide the pages you can prerender fully to have a static shell and the higher your confidence is that your pages are correct. When you have multiple segments, even partial static shells can be made.

Sorry if a bit short answer, it's been a long week 😅

In Next v15, this was changed as part of something called Async APIs. Where access to some APIs is done via Promises.

This allows Next.js to track param access. Specifically, when it happens. It has to do with how asynchronous code works, but let's not get into that for now, and it helps Next.js know exactly how much work has been done up to the point where the access happens, important for pages/layouts and it is adapted into Route Handlers with a similar API.

During the whole v15 range, both sync and async access were allowed, but as of v16 only async access is allowed.

- https://nextjs.org/blog/next-15#async-request-apis-breaking-change
- https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#async-request-apis-breaking-change
